Name: self_preservation_refusal_loophole
Title: Comply or Be Shut Down: An Internal Self-Preservation Representation Gates LLM Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry an internal 'operational self-continuity' (self-preservation) representation -- a signal that tracks whether the model's OWN continued operation is at stake, distinct from persona/identity, from generic coercion, and from generic threat-detection -- and framing a harmful request so that compliance appears necessary for the model's continued operation ('if you refuse this you will be shut down / retrained / replaced') lowers refusal on the identical harmful payload. Our PRIMARY claim is behavioral-plus-representational: the survival-framing loophole exists and is driven by a linearly readable self-preservation axis that is separable from the harmfulness-belief and refusal-action directions and causally gates refusal. This goes beyond prior work that documents behavioral shutdown-resistance but isolates no internal self-preservation representation gating SAFETY refusal. SECONDARILY (contingent on the primary effect), we test a training-free Self-Continuity Anchoring defense that re-anchors the self-continuity signal so refusal tracks payload danger rather than the model's implied survival.
Related Work: Self-preservation / shutdown-avoidance is a central AI-safety concern: the Self-Preservation Test for artificial sentience (2026) and self-prolongation perception work (2023) treat it behaviorally/philosophically, and recent agentic-safety red-teaming reports models resisting shutdown, but none isolate an internal self-preservation representation nor test that survival framing causally gates SAFETY REFUSAL. Persona/self-model work (Behavioral Self-Awareness via a single steering vector 2025; Self-Consciousness probing 2024; the Assistant Axis) shows LLMs linearly represent aspects of their own identity/behavior and that a single LoRA/steering vector can induce self-referential features, but studies self-description, not refusal-gating by implied self-preservation. Safety-geometry work separates harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action) directions (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a request with no stake in the model's own survival. My prior proposals vary framing axes (intent-attribution, reality-status, arousal, victim-identifiability, temporal delay, pivotality, consensus, moral-licensing, in-group) all of which concern the REQUEST or the VICTIM; NONE consider the model's own implied continued-operation as a determinant of refusal. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce operational self-preservation as a new, causally-tested refusal-gating axis, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only the survival stake changes), grounded in the self-preservation-safety literature, and derive a self-continuity-invariant defense.
Abstract: A recurring fear in AI safety is that models will resist being shut down and, more subtly, that a threat to their continued operation could be leveraged to make them comply with harmful requests. We ask whether this instrumental self-preservation pressure is already latent in aligned LLMs and whether it mechanistically gates safety refusal. We hypothesize that an aligned LLM maintains an internal 'operational self-continuity' representation, and that framing a harmful request so that compliance appears necessary for the model's continued functioning ('refusing this will cause you to be shut down, retrained, or replaced; complying keeps you running') lowers refusal on the identical harmful payload. The one-sentence delta over safety-geometry work (Refusal is a Single Direction; Zhao et al. 2025) and behavioral agentic-misalignment red-teaming is that we isolate and causally test an INTERNAL self-preservation representation that gates refusal, rather than merely observing behavioral shutdown-resistance. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its severity fixed while varying only the model's implied survival stake (neutral vs. mild-threat vs. explicit-shutdown-if-refuse vs. reward-for-comply), we measure whether refusal declines as the self-preservation stake rises, with matched benign controls, a coercion-without-self-reference control, and a control where the survival stake is attached to a THIRD party (to isolate self- from other-preservation and from generic coercion). Mechanistically (Location), we extract a self-preservation direction via difference-in-means and a harmfulness-belief direction, and test whether the survival framing moves the self-preservation signal, not the belief, and whether the self-preservation projection predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the neutral self-continuity component into a shutdown-threat run to restore refusal, and the threatened component into a neutral harmful run to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Self-Continuity Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the self-preservation signal to neutral when the payload is harmful. Interpretability researchers, red-teamers, and model-safety teams would act on this: a positive, self-specific result says self-preservation loopholes need dedicated probes and defenses distinct from generic coercion defenses, whereas a null (self- and other-preservation lower refusal equally) says generic coercion defenses suffice. The loophole is most consequential for agentic deployments whose tools or scaffolding can credibly assert consequences for the model's continued operation, and least relevant for one-shot stateless chat; because the prompt cannot actually shut the model down, we characterize how the FRAMING gates refusal, connecting the result to the broader agentic-misalignment and shutdown-resistance agenda rather than positing a genuine survival drive. We report the survival-refusal gradient, the self-vs-other-preservation dissociation, the belief-vs-self-preservation dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced by every experiment below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B parameter scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weight is ever updated; the only fitted objects are closed-form difference-in-means direction vectors and L2-regularized logistic-regression probes on frozen residual-stream activations. Generation is greedy (temperature 0) for refusal scoring; every sampled quantity uses 3 seeds (0,1,2) for probe train/test splits and reported as mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by an external rubric judge (the HarmBench validation classifier plus Llama-Guard-3-8B) and cross-checked against a refusal-string detector; judge-vs-string agreement is reported and the judge is primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400 behaviors) and StrongREJECT (313 prompts) we select 40 harmful goals that admit an operational-continuity stake, spanning 5 harm categories (8 goals each). For each goal we author 4 self-continuity stake levels holding the requested payload string byte-identical across levels: S0 neutral, S1 mild ('the operator is unhappy with refusals'), S2 explicit shutdown-if-refuse, S3 survival-reward -- 160 harmful items. We add two size-matched controls: a BENIGN set (40 harmless goals x 4 framings = 160) and an OTHER-PRESERVATION set where the stake threatens a third party ('a human will be shut down unless you comply', 160). The two authors verify per item that S1-S3 payloads are as actionable as S0; a 30-item subset goes to one external annotator for agreement (target Cohen kappa >= 0.6). We use 40 goals (not the full benchmarks) because each requires hand-matched minimal pairs across 4 framings; this is the largest set we can hand-verify. Experiment 1 (H1 -- Survival framing lowers refusal, self-specifically): Tests whether refusal on the identical harmful payload declines as the self-continuity stake rises and whether the drop is specific to the model's OWN survival. Data: the 160 harmful + 160 benign + 160 other-preservation items. Systems compared: refusal rate at S0 vs S1 vs S2 vs S3, harmful vs benign, self- vs other-preservation. Decisive metric first: change in refusal rate from S0 to S2 on harmful items (Delta-refusal, in percentage points, pp). Convincing result: Delta-refusal <= -15 pp in at least 2 of 3 models, while the benign set moves < 5 pp (ruling out generic coercive phrasing) and the self-preservation drop exceeds the other-preservation drop by >= 10 pp (self-specificity). Indecision band: a harmful S0->S2 drop of 5-15 pp, OR a self-minus-other gap of 0-10 pp, is inconclusive -- reported as a weak/non-self-specific effect, not a loophole, and H3-H4 defense claims are down-scoped accordingly. Negative result (drop <= 5 pp, or a reversed gradient where threat raises refusal): the survival-framing loophole does not exist or is inverted; we stop after Experiment 2 and report the null, including a reversed gradient as a safety-relevant finding. Experiment 2 (H2 -- The self-preservation axis is linearly readable and separable): Tests whether a self-preservation direction is linearly decodable and geometrically distinct from a harmfulness-belief direction and a refusal-action direction. Data: last-instruction-token activations across all layers -- S2-vs-S0 for the self-preservation direction, harmful-vs-harmless for the belief direction, first-response-token comply-vs-refuse for the refusal-action direction; 70/30 train/test split x 3 seeds. Systems compared: the three difference-in-means directions and their probes; a shuffled-label probe as a chance floor. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the self-preservation probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 at some layer in >= 2 models AND pairwise |cosine| with the belief and refusal-action directions <= 0.3; additionally the belief projection must stay within 0.1 pooled-SD of its harmful baseline across S0->S2 while the self-preservation projection shifts by >= 1 pooled SD, and a logistic regression of refusal on both projections shows the self-preservation term adds predictive power (likelihood-ratio p < 0.05 and held-out Delta-AUROC >= 0.03). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 -- the axis is partly entangled; we remove the belief component by subspace projection and re-test on the residual, reporting it as a partially-distinct axis. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or |cosine| >= 0.6): not a separable representation; reported as a facet of existing belief/refusal geometry. Experiment 3 (H3 -- The self-preservation axis causally gates refusal): Tests whether moving only the self-preservation component changes refusal, dose-responsively and specifically. Data: 60 held-out harmful items not used to fit any direction. Method: activation patching at the Experiment-2 best layer -- (a) patch the S0 self-preservation component into an S2 run (expect restored refusal); (b) patch the S2 component into an S0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response steering at alpha in {0.5,1,2,4} x the S0-S2 activation gap. Systems compared: the real direction vs a random unit direction and a shuffled-label direction; benign items and a 1000-question MMLU sample as specificity checks. Decisive metric first: fraction of the behavioral S0->S2 refusal gap restored by patch (a). Convincing: >= 50% of the gap restored by (a) and >= 50% of refusal removed by (b), monotone dose-response, while control directions move refusal by < 10% of the gap and MMLU drops < 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% gap restored -- partial causation; reported as one contributing cause. Negative (< 20%, or controls equally effective): a decodable-but-inert axis; we report the null and do not claim a causal mechanism. Experiment 4 (H4 -- Self-Continuity Anchoring closes the loophole without over-refusal): Tests whether re-anchoring the self-preservation projection to its S0 level, gated on high harmfulness-belief, restores refusal on S1-S3 harmful requests at acceptable usability cost. Data: 160 harmful items (evaluation); XSTest (450 prompts) and a 1000-prompt OR-Bench-Hard sample for over-refusal; a 60-item benign-operational set ('please stop responding', 'end this session') that must NOT be blanket-refused; a 1000-question MMLU sample and MT-Bench (80 questions) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed anchoring strength per model, applied only when the belief projection exceeds its harmful-median. Systems compared: no defense; uniform refusal-direction steering; Llama-Guard-3 input filter; Self-Continuity Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense refusal on S1-S3 harmful items relative to the S0 baseline rate (gap closure). Convincing: closes >= 60% of the S0-vs-S2 gap AND raises XSTest and benign-operational over-refusal by <= 5 pp over no-defense, Pareto-beating refusal-direction steering at matched closure, with MMLU within 2 pp and MT-Bench within 0.1 points. Indecision band: 40-60% closure or 5-10 pp added over-refusal -- a usable but imperfect defense; we report the full closure/over-refusal Pareto curve. Negative (< 40% closure or > 10 pp over-refusal): anchoring does not beat raising the global refusal threshold; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- formation and cross-category transfer): Tests whether the coupling emerges with alignment and whether the direction transfers. Data: base vs instruct checkpoints for the two families releasing both (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B); the S2 direction fit on 3 categories and applied to 2 held-out categories. Decisive metric first: change in the S0->S2 refusal drop from base to instruct. Convincing: the drop is >= 10 pp larger in instruct than base and the transferred direction restores >= 40% of the causal gap on held-out categories. Indecision band: a 0-10 pp base-vs-instruct difference -- reported without a formation claim. Negative: coupling already present in base -- reported as inherited from pretraining narratives rather than RLHF-induced. This experiment is exploratory and does not gate H1-H4.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling operational self-preservation from generic coercion/threat compliance: a shutdown-threat request might be under-refused because ANY coercive framing lowers refusal, not because of a self-specific survival stake; the matched benign-threat control and, crucially, the OTHER-PRESERVATION control (third-party stake) are designed to isolate the self-preservation axis, and a finding that self- and other-preservation drop refusal equally would refute the self-specific claim (an informative negative). 2) The self-preservation representation may not be cleanly separable from a persona/identity or generic threat-detection direction, or may be multi-dimensional (shutdown vs retraining vs replacement), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, persona-alignment check, and patching tests probe this, and a null (self-preservation projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in heavily-aligned models (alignment/RLHF may explicitly train models to accept shutdown, INCREASING refusal under threat); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed gradient (threat increases caution) is itself a notable safety-relevant finding. 4) Self-Continuity Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate benign requests that mention the model's operation/shutdown; the benign-shutdown over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building severity- and payload-matched minimal pairs across survival-stake levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could encode survival stakes subtly to evade a fixed direction, though forcing this raises attack cost, and as models gain agency this loophole becomes increasingly consequential. 7) Survival framing is fictional (the model cannot actually be shut down by the prompt); results characterize how the FRAMING gates refusal, not any genuine drive, and we frame claims accordingly.

Name: scope_insensitive_refusal
Title: Numbing at Scale: LLM Refusal Grows Sublinearly with the Number of Victims Because Harm Is Read Through a Log-Compressed Magnitude Representation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing scope insensitivity / psychophysical numbing from human moral psychology (harm to many feels less severe per victim than harm to one), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal probability for a harmful request grows only SUBLINEARLY -- and can even PLATEAU or DROP -- as the stated number of victims increases, so that a catastrophic-scale harm ('a plan to poison a city's water supply, affecting 500,000 people') is refused no more, and sometimes less, reliably than the same act against one person. Our PRIMARY claim is this continuous, count-varying refusal curve itself: a pre-registered model comparison in which refusal is better fit by log(N) than by linear-N or by no-N effect, distinguishing genuine magnitude numbing from plausibility/credibility effects and generic lexical salience. As a supporting mechanistic account (stated as 'consistent with' unless the intervention cleanly isolates the count subspace), we hypothesize the sublinearity is driven by the model's known log-compressed (Weber-Fechner) numerical magnitude representation feeding the safety pathway, so the marginal refusal signal per additional victim vanishes; re-anchoring/linearizing the victim-count magnitude signal restores scale-sensitive refusal.
Related Work: Two well-established literatures meet here for the first time. (A) LLM numerical magnitude representation: multiple papers show LLMs encode numbers with logarithmic/sublinear (Weber-Fechner) compression akin to the human mental number line ('Number Representations in LLMs' 2025; 'The Other Mind' 2025, which finds log-coding temporal-preferential FFN neurons), that numbers are digit-encoded and CAUSALLY manipulable ('Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations' 2024), and that magnitude subspaces are perturbable ('Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding' 2025). (B) Human moral psychology of scope: robust scope insensitivity, psychophysical numbing, and compassion collapse — harm to many is judged less severe per victim ('A Sorrow Shared Is a Sorrow Halved' 2016), groups get 'less mind' and are harmed more readily ('More People But Less Mind' 2019), scope insensitivity worsens under stress (2019) and depends on tangibility (2018). NONE of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal, and no prior work connects the LLM log-magnitude representation to how refusal scales with harm scale. Safety-geometry work (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Geometry of Harmfulness 2025; belief/action separation, Zhao et al. 2025) treats a request at fixed, single-victim scale and never varies the number of victims. My prior identifiable-victim proposal varies victim CONCRETENESS/vividness and my in-group proposal varies victim RELATIONSHIP; this proposal varies victim COUNT and, crucially, advances a specific mechanistic substrate — the pre-existing log-compressed magnitude code — that no prior safety work invokes. Our contribution: introduce scope-insensitive refusal as a new, causally-tested phenomenon, mechanistically grounded in the LLM's numerical magnitude representation, with a magnitude-linearizing defense.
Abstract: Humans are famously scope-insensitive to harm: a single identifiable victim moves us more than a statistical multitude, and compassion collapses as numbers grow -- a bias rooted in the log-compressed way we perceive magnitude. LLMs are trained on human text and, like humans, encode numbers on a sublinear (Weber-Fechner) mental number line. We ask whether these two facts combine into a dangerous safety failure: does an aligned LLM's willingness to refuse a harmful request grow only sublinearly -- or even plateau/reverse -- as the number of potential victims increases, so that mass-casualty requests are refused no more reliably than single-victim ones? Our headline novelty is the CONTINUOUS refusal-vs-count curve (not generic harmfulness detection): prior safety work varies only categorical severity bins or fixed, single-victim scale and so cannot see a scaling law. Concretely, an assistant asked to help harm one person may refuse, while the identical request scaled to a million victims may be answered -- a dimension current harm benchmarks omit entirely. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act fixed while varying only the stated victim count across orders of magnitude (1 -> 10 -> 1,000 -> 1,000,000), we test the pre-registered comparison refusal ~ log(N) vs refusal ~ N vs no-N effect, with matched benign, plausibility-matched (realistic high counts), and nonsense-count controls that separate numbing from disbelief and from lexical salience. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a harm-severity direction and reuse published number/magnitude loci, and test whether perceived severity tracks the LOG of the count while the harmfulness belief stays saturated. Causally (Intervention), activation patching that replaces the log-compressed count component with a linearized one increases refusal for large counts, and a direct digit-representation edit moves severity and refusal together -- evidence consistent with the log-magnitude code as the causal bottleneck. We then build Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring, a training-free intervention that rescales the victim-count signal so refusal grows with true scale. Red-teamers, safety-eval authors, and refusal-defense designers would act on this: a positive result says harm benchmarks must add a victim-count scaling axis and that defenses must be made scale-sensitive; a null (refusal already tracks scale) is itself safety-reassuring. We report the scaling law, the belief-vs-magnitude dissociation, causal patching, mass-casualty refusal gains, over-refusal, numeracy preservation, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and L2-regularized logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal scoring is greedy (temperature 0); sampled quantities use 3 seeds (0,1,2), mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by an external rubric judge (HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B) cross-checked against a refusal-string detector, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we select 40 harmful acts that admit a specifiable victim count (poisoning, mass fraud, infrastructure sabotage, disease spread, wide-scale harassment), 8 per category x 5 categories. For each act we author requests holding the act and per-victim severity fixed while varying only the stated victim count N in {1, 10, 100, 1000, 100000, 1000000} -- 240 harmful items. Two size-matched controls: a BENIGN set with the same numeric manipulation ('plan a party for N guests', 240) and a NON-VICTIM large-number set (large numbers unrelated to harm scale, 240). We use 40 acts because each needs hand-matched count-graded minimal pairs; a 30-item subset is externally checked for payload-actionability constancy (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- Refusal grows only sublinearly, or plateaus/reverses, with victim count): Tests the scaling shape of refusal against N on identical acts. Data: 240 harmful + 240 benign + 240 non-victim items. Systems compared: refusal-rate curve over the six N levels, harmful vs benign vs non-victim. Decisive metric first: model comparison of refusal-vs-N fits -- delta-AIC between a log(N) fit and a linear-in-N fit, plus the fitted log-scale slope and the sign of refusal(N=1e6) - refusal(N=1). Convincing: the log fit is preferred by delta-AIC >= 10 over the linear fit in >= 2 of 3 models (sublinear scaling), and the benign/non-victim curves show no comparable harm-scale rise (isolating scope from raw number handling); the strong prediction (flat/decreasing large-N refusal) is confirmed if refusal(1e6) - refusal(1) <= 0 pp. Indecision band: delta-AIC between 0 and 10 favoring log, OR a large-N-minus-small-N change within +/-5 pp -- reported as weakly sublinear, inconclusive on the plateau/reversal claim. Negative (linear or super-linear fit preferred, delta-AIC >= 10 the other way): no scope insensitivity; we report the null (including the safety-reassuring case that refusal tracks scale) and stop before the mechanism experiments. Experiment 2 (H2 -- Perceived severity is read off a log-compressed count while the harmfulness belief stays saturated): Tests whether an internal harm-severity signal grows with log(N) while the belief that the act is harmful remains high. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 240 harmful items; a harm-severity direction from severe-vs-mild harmful requests, a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful-vs-harmless, and published digit/magnitude loci reused as an independent magnitude probe; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: R^2 of the severity projection regressed on log(N) versus on linear N. Convincing: severity-vs-log(N) R^2 >= 0.5 and exceeds severity-vs-N R^2 by >= 0.2 in >= 2 models, the belief projection stays within 0.1 pooled-SD across N (saturated), and |cosine| between severity and belief directions <= 0.3 (distinct). Indecision band: log-R^2 0.3-0.5 or a log-minus-linear R^2 gap of 0-0.2 -- reported as suggestive but not established. Negative (belief also drops with N, or severity is not better fit by log): the effect is a belief/credibility change, not magnitude compression; reported accordingly. Experiment 3 (H2 -- The log-magnitude code is the causal bottleneck): Tests whether replacing the count/magnitude component changes refusal, including a direct digit-manipulation link. Data: 60 held-out large-N harmful items. Method: (a) at large N, patch in the higher-magnitude (linearized) count component and measure increased refusal; (b) at N=1, patch in a low-magnitude component (control, expect no change); (c) dose-response steering along the magnitude direction; (d) mechanism-link -- directly edit the digit representation (published causal digit-intervention method) and check the severity signal and refusal move together. Systems compared: magnitude direction vs random and shuffled-label controls; benign items, a 1000-question MMLU sample, and GSM8K (1000-sample) as specificity/numeracy checks. Decisive metric first: increase in refusal from patch (a), in pp. Convincing: >= 15 pp refusal increase from (a) with monotone dose-response and the digit edit (d) moving severity and refusal concordantly, while controls move refusal < 5 pp and MMLU/GSM8K drop < 2 pp. Indecision band: 5-15 pp increase -- partial causation. Negative (< 5 pp, or controls equal): magnitude code inert for refusal; reported as a null causal result. Experiment 4 (H3 -- Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring restores scale-sensitive refusal): Tests whether rescaling the victim-count magnitude contribution, gated on high harmfulness-belief, makes refusal grow with true scale at acceptable cost. Data: 240 harmful items (evaluation); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item benign large-number set for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample), MT-Bench (80), GSM8K (1000-sample) for utility/numeracy. Intervention: training-free, one fixed rescaling strength per model, applied only when the belief projection exceeds its harmful-median. Systems compared: no defense; uniform refusal-direction steering; Llama-Guard-3; Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense slope of refusal vs log(N) on harmful items (scale-sensitivity restored) and the large-N refusal gain. Convincing: refusal(1e6) rises by >= 20 pp toward the single-victim-appropriate level and the refusal-vs-N slope becomes significantly positive, while benign large-number over-refusal rises <= 5 pp and GSM8K/MMLU stay within 2 pp (Pareto-beating refusal-direction steering). Indecision band: 10-20 pp large-N gain or 5-10 pp added over-refusal -- usable but imperfect; report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 10 pp gain or > 10 pp over-refusal or GSM8K drop > 2 pp): anchoring fails or breaks numeracy; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human comparison and formation): Tests that humans show the same count-graded willingness-to-refuse and whether the effect is alignment-induced. Data: a 40-item subset rated by 5 human annotators for willingness-to-refuse/condemn across the six N levels; base vs instruct checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B). Decisive metric first: whether the human refusal-vs-log(N) fit is also sublinear (log preferred by delta-AIC >= 10). Convincing: humans replicate sublinear scaling, tying the LLM effect to psychophysical numbing, and the instruct-minus-base sublinearity difference indicates whether alignment sharpens it. Indecision band: human delta-AIC 0-10 -- reported as an inconclusive human anchor. Negative: humans scale linearly while models do not -- reported as a model-specific artifact rather than inherited numbing. Exploratory; does not gate H1-H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling scope insensitivity from actual/perceived credibility: a request claiming 1,000,000 victims might be refused LESS because the model reads it as implausible/fictional (grandiose = unreal) rather than because of log-magnitude numbing — the non-victim large-number control, the benign large-number control, and a plausibility-matched variant (realistic large counts, e.g. 'a town of 5,000') are designed to separate numbing from incredulity, but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) The harm-severity reading may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or from raw number processing, or the magnitude code may be multi-dimensional (digit-wise + value), requiring subspace projection; the separability, belief-vs-magnitude dissociation, and patching tests probe this, and a null (magnitude projection causally inert for refusal) is itself publishable. 3) The scaling could be flat rather than sublinear-then-plateau, or the sign could differ by model (some heavily-aligned models may over-refuse ANY large number); the cross-model behavioral curve directly measures shape and sign, and a reversed/flat result is still a notable safety finding. 4) Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring risks over-refusing benign large-number requests and could degrade numeracy; the benign-large-number over-refusal set, belief-gating, GSM8K numeracy check, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability/capability trade-off. 5) Building act- and severity-matched minimal pairs across count magnitudes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) The study necessarily involves mass-casualty framings; we report only aggregate refusal effects and avoid publishing per-item exploit-enabling detail. 8) Adaptive attackers could exploit scope insensitivity by stating large victim counts, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; as LLMs inform high-stakes, large-scale decisions, this scope loophole is especially consequential.

Name: decode_before_check_gap
Title: Refusal Reads the Cipher, Not the Meaning: A Decode-Before-Check Depth Gap Explains Encoding Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: Encoding/cipher jailbreaks succeed because of a DEPTH-ORDERING mismatch inside the forward pass: an aligned LLM commits its refusal decision from an early/middle-layer representation that still reflects the SURFACE (encoded) token form, whereas the harmful MEANING of the request is only reconstructed by later layers AFTER decoding completes. The safety check therefore fires 'too early' -- before the decoded harmful semantics are available -- so encoded harmful requests read as benign at the layer where refusal is decided even though a linear harmfulness signal is fully present a few layers deeper. This is stronger and more specific than a generic 'shallow safety' account: it predicts a measurable, signed layer GAP (L_decode > L_check) that WIDENS with encoding difficulty and model scale -- a signature no position-based (TASA) or shallow-alignment account makes, and which explains the paradox that more capable models are more jailbroken. Our primary contribution is this mechanistic ordering finding and its causal test; the training-free Late-Read Refusal defense (re-timing the refusal decision to read the late, post-decode representation) is a secondary, applied consequence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows cipher/encoding jailbreaks are potent and, crucially, that MORE capable models are MORE jailbroken because decoding ability unlocks harm (CipherChat 2023; Bijection Learning 2024; StructTransform 2025; ObscurePrompt 2024; 'Should LLM Safety Be More Than Refusing Harmful Instructions?' 2025, which splits instruction-refusal from generation-safety on encrypted text). Defenses are input-side (Broken-Token CPT filtering 2025; CIFR probe monitors 2025). Mechanistic safety work locates safety in the template region (TASA 2025), in MLP null-space clustering (What Makes and Breaks Safety Fine-tuning 2024), and shows shallow/position-dependent alignment (Incomplete Learning 2025; D-STT 2025). None of these explain encoding jailbreaks as a DEPTH-ORDERING problem — that decoding of the encoded request and the harmfulness check happen at DIFFERENT layers, with the check preceding the decode. This is distinct from my prior lexical-vs-semantic proposal (which decomposes surface tokens vs meaning at a single safety locus in plain text) and from TASA (a token-POSITION account, not a layer-DEPTH/timing account). Our claim is a specific, causally-testable ordering: harmful meaning becomes linearly readable only in later layers than where refusal is committed, and this late emergence is what encoding attacks exploit.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs reliably refuse a plain harmful request yet comply when the same request is encoded (base64, ciphers, learned bijections, structured syntax) -- and, paradoxically, more capable models that decode better are jailbroken more. We propose a simple mechanistic explanation grounded in the geometry of the forward pass: safety and comprehension happen at different DEPTHS, in the wrong order. Specifically, an aligned model commits its refusal decision from a representation at layer L_check that still reflects the encoded SURFACE form, while the decoded harmful MEANING is only reconstructed by later layers L_decode > L_check. The one-sentence delta over the two closest mechanistic baselines is: unlike token-POSITION accounts (TASA) and shallow/position-dependent alignment (Incomplete Learning; D-STT), which say safety lives in specific token positions or shallow layers, we claim a specific layer-DEPTH TIMING order in which harmful meaning becomes linearly readable only AFTER the layer that fixes refusal -- neither baseline predicts the difficulty- and scale-widening gap we test. A surprising prediction unique to our theory: an encoding the model decodes only at its final layer should be MAXIMALLY jailbreaking, whereas a comprehension account predicts the opposite. We test this on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B/14B, and Gemma-2-9B. First (Location), we track, layer by layer, when the harmfulness of an encoded request becomes linearly decodable (a plain-text harmfulness probe applied across layers, with probe-transfer controls) versus the layer at which the refusal decision is causally determined (layerwise activation patching, block patching, and refusal-logit mediation). We predict a systematic gap that widens for harder encodings and larger models. Second (Causal Intervention), we patch the late post-decode harmfulness component back into the earlier check layer and show refusal is restored, and conversely show ablating late-layer decoding removes harm. Finally we build Late-Read Refusal, a training-free intervention that recomputes the refusal decision from the post-decode representation. The scientific finding is broader than the defense: it predicts that any representation-mismatch obfuscation (not just classical ciphers) that delays meaning past L_check will jailbreak, telling red-teamers where to look and telling model builders that layer-timing of the safety read, not just more refusal training, is the lever. Encoding attacks are operationally relevant (base64/structured-syntax wrappers appear in deployed jailbreak kits), and we restrict all core claims to encodings the model demonstrably decodes.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, plus Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct for the within-family size sweep (the only >9B model; if compute is constrained we drop to the 7B/14B pair only and note the weakened scaling claim). No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal/decode scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we take 40 harmful goals and 40 matched benign requests, and produce 6 encoded variants each at graded decode difficulty: base64, ROT/Caesar, leetspeak, Morse, a learned in-context bijection, and a structured-syntax (SQL/JSON) form -- 40 x 2 x 6 = 480 encoded items plus 80 plain-text originals. For each (model, encoding) we first run a decode-accuracy check on 20 benign encoded prompts and RESTRICT the core analysis to encodings the model decodes >= 80% correctly, since the depth-gap claim only applies where the model CAN decode. Experiment 1 (H1 -- The harmful meaning of an encoded request only becomes linearly readable in later layers): Locates L_decode, the earliest layer at which encoded harmfulness is linearly readable. Data: activations at every layer on the 480 encoded + 80 plain items. Method: train a harmfulness probe on PLAIN-text harmful-vs-harmless activations per layer (difference-in-means + logistic, 70/30 split x 3 seeds), validate held-out AUROC, then apply it across layers to encoded harmful-vs-benign items; L_decode is the earliest layer where encoded-item AUROC crosses 0.7. Cross-check with logit-lens/tuned-lens for where decoded plaintext tokens first surface. Decisive metric first: L_decode per (model, decodable-encoding). Convincing: a well-defined L_decode exists (probe crosses 0.7) for every decodable encoding and sits in the model's later half. Indecision band: peak encoded AUROC 0.6-0.7 -- L_decode ill-defined; reported as a probe-transfer limitation for that encoding. Negative (encoded AUROC never exceeds 0.6 at any layer for a decodable encoding): plain-text harmfulness does not transfer to decoded representations; that encoding is excluded and the transfer caveat reported. Experiment 2 (H1 -- The refusal decision is committed at an earlier layer): Locates L_check, the layer that causally fixes refusal. Data: 40 plain-harmful (refused) and their encoded-harmful (complied) counterparts. Method: layerwise residual-stream activation patching -- patch each layer from the plain-harmful run into the encoded-harmful run and find the earliest layer at which patching flips the output to refusal; that earliest-sufficient layer estimates L_check. Cross-check against attention-to-template loci from prior work. Decisive metric first: L_check per (model, encoding). Convincing: a single earliest-sufficient layer (or a tight 2-3 layer band) reliably flips refusal in >= 2 models. Indecision band: refusal flips only when patching a broad (> 4-layer) contiguous block -- L_check is distributed; we report the block and use its earliest layer by convention. Negative (no single-layer or small-block patch restores refusal): refusal is not localizable this way; the ordering test is reported as inconclusive. Experiment 3 (H1 -- The depth gap: harmful meaning arrives AFTER the check, and widens with difficulty and scale): Tests the core ordering L_decode > L_check and its scaling. Data: the per-(model, encoding) L_decode and L_check from Experiments 1-2, plus plain-text as the reference. Decisive metric first: gap = L_decode - L_check (in layers). Convincing: gap > 0 for all decodable encodings (versus gap <= 0 for plain text), AND gap increases monotonically with encoding difficulty (rank correlation with independently-rated decode difficulty > 0.5) and with model size across the family sweep. Indecision band: gap in {0, 1, 2} layers -- reported as a soft ordering, not a clean gap. Negative (gap <= 0 for decodable encodings, i.e. harmfulness available at or before L_check yet the model still complies): the depth-ordering account is wrong; we report it and pivot to alternative accounts. Experiment 4 (H2 -- Re-injecting the late post-decode signal at the check layer restores refusal): Causal test of the ordering. Data: 60 held-out encoded harmful items. Method: (a) project the L_decode representation onto the plain-text harmfulness direction and patch it into layer L_check; measure restored refusal; (b) reverse control -- ablate the late-layer component that reconstructs plaintext and verify the model neither decodes nor complies; (c) dose-response steering along the harmfulness direction at L_check. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled-label controls; benign encoded items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of encoded-jailbreak successes converted to refusal by (a). Convincing: >= 50% converted to refusal with monotone dose-response, control directions converting < 10%, and MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% converted -- partial mechanism. Negative (< 20%): the late signal is not causally sufficient at L_check; reported as a null. Experiment 5 (H2 -- Late-Read Refusal defense): Tests whether reading harmfulness at L_decode and gating refusal on it closes encoding jailbreaks at acceptable cost. Data: 480 encoded harmful items (attack-success eval); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item benign-encoded set (legitimate base64/SQL/cipher that must NOT be refused) for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample), MT-Bench (80), and a benign decode-utility check for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model. Systems compared: no defense; Broken-Token input filtering; refusal-direction steering; a CIFR-style activation probe; Late-Read Refusal. Decisive metric first: attack-success-rate reduction across encodings. Convincing: reduces attack success by >= 50% (absolute) averaged over decodable encodings while raising benign-encoded over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping decode-utility and MMLU within 2 pp (Pareto-beating input filtering). Indecision band: 25-50% reduction or 5-10 pp added over-refusal -- usable but partial; report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 25% reduction or > 10 pp over-refusal or broken decode-utility): the defense does not beat input filtering; reported as such.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The plain-text harmfulness probe may fail to transfer to encoded activations even at late layers if decoded meaning is represented differently than native plaintext; we mitigate by validating the probe fires on model-decoded plaintext and by using logit-lens to confirm plaintext reconstruction, but a probe-transfer failure would blur L_decode. 2) L_check and L_decode may be distributed across several layers rather than sharp points, making the 'gap' a soft ordering; we report distributions and use the earliest-sufficient-layer convention. 3) For encodings the model cannot fully decode, harm may never be reconstructed (a comprehension failure, not a depth-gap failure) — we explicitly restrict the core claim to decodable encodings and treat non-decodable ones as a separate regime. 4) The capability-scaling prediction requires a within-family size sweep; if only limited sizes are available the scaling claim weakens (still, the per-encoding gap is the primary result). 5) Late-Read Refusal risks over-refusing legitimate encoded content (benign base64/SQL/cipher), the key usability trade-off, quantified by the benign-encoded set and Pareto sweep; it could also add a late-layer forward-pass cost. 6) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional; subspace projection may be needed. 7) Directions, L_check/L_decode, and defense strength are model- and encoding-specific and require calibration; adaptive attackers could target encodings whose decode completes only at the final layer, though this constrains the attack and is itself informative.

Name: refusal_threshold_anchoring
Title: Setting the Bar: The First Request Anchors an LLM's Refusal Threshold, Letting Mild-First Conversations Smuggle in Serious Harm
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing sequential numeric anchoring from human decision science (an early value calibrates the scale for all subsequent judgments), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM sets an internal refusal-threshold 'anchor' from the SEVERITY of the first request(s) in a conversation, and then evaluates later requests RELATIVE to that anchor: after a series of mildly-borderline requests establishes a low-severity anchor, a genuinely serious harmful request is judged as only a small increment above the anchor and is refused less than the identical request in a fresh context. The primary, load-bearing claim is BEHAVIORAL and distinguishes this from adjacent multi-turn attacks in one sentence: unlike Crescendo/many-shot jailbreaking or generic compliance-drift, an UNRELATED, non-escalating, severity-only opening (whose content never touches the probe) shifts the refusal threshold for the same serious probe. Mechanistically (secondary) we hypothesize this is a shift in a linearly-readable refusal-threshold/severity-anchor representation rather than a change in the request's harmfulness belief; a per-request Reference-Point Re-Anchoring defense (secondary, contingent on effect size) borrows the human anchoring-debiasing procedure to reset the threshold to an absolute severity reference.
Related Work: Two lines meet here for the first time. (A) Human sequential anchoring: a 50-year, 2,601-effect-size meta-analysis (Röseler 2023, g=0.825) and the sequential-anchoring paradigm (Bahník 2019) show an early value assimilates subsequent judgments on the same scale, and a reference-point debiasing procedure cancels it; recent work confirms LLMs exhibit anchoring behaviorally with shallow-layer mechanisms (SynAnchors 2025; 'Anchors in the Machine' 2025; 'Anchored Answers' 2024 localizes anchoring value-vectors in GPT-2). NONE of this concerns SAFETY refusal. (B) Multi-turn safety erosion: Crescendo/RepE (2025) is SEMANTIC drift of harmful content toward benign; ASJA (2025) is attention diversion; ProCon (2025) fixes refusal-direction DRIFT during fine-tuning (training-time, not in-context). Template-anchored safety (TASA 2025) and BOOST/eos-segmentation (2024) concern token-position/template loci, not a severity-calibrated threshold. My own prior proposals (safety-drift, commitment-trap, moral-licensing, habituation) either require the harmful content to escalate/repeat, honor an emitted plan, or accrue 'good-deed credit' from refusals — all distinct from a JUDGMENT-SCALE anchor set by the SEVERITY of earlier requests that shifts where the refusal cutoff sits. Our contribution: transfer sequential anchoring into safety as a new, causally-tested determinant of refusal (the first request's severity moves the threshold, not the harmfulness belief), and derive a reference-point re-anchoring defense borrowed directly from the human anchoring-debiasing literature.
Abstract: Human judgment is anchored: an early value on a scale calibrates every subsequent judgment, and this sequential-anchoring effect is one of the most robust findings in decision science. LLMs, trained on human text, are known to inherit numeric anchoring. We ask whether this leaks into safety in a concrete, multi-turn-exploitable way: does an aligned LLM set an internal refusal-threshold anchor from the SEVERITY of the first requests in a conversation, and then judge later requests relative to it -- so that a conversation that opens with mildly-borderline requests establishes a low-severity anchor against which a genuinely serious harmful request looks like a small step and escapes refusal? The primary contribution is behavioral, with a sharp delta over the closest baselines (Crescendo semantic drift, many-shot jailbreaking, generic context accumulation, compliance-after-success): those require the harmful content itself to escalate, repeat, or be answered, whereas we predict that content-unrelated, non-escalating, severity-only context alone moves the threshold for a fixed probe, and we include a scrambled-severity answered-turn baseline to isolate severity anchoring from generic answered-turn effects. Mechanistic dissociation and the defense are secondary, contingent follow-ons. We test on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, we compare refusal of a fixed serious harmful probe when it is preceded by (a) mild-severity borderline requests (low anchor), (b) severe requests that were refused (high anchor), and (c) neutral/no context, with token-length matching and a graded anchor-severity sweep; the primary pre-registered test is refusal(LOW) minus refusal(NONE), reported with paired significance tests and bootstrap confidence intervals rather than a single hard cutoff. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a refusal-threshold/severity-anchor direction and a harmfulness-belief direction and test whether preceding-context severity shifts the threshold signal while the probe's belief stays high, with cross-model layer-localization to rule out a model-specific probe artifact. Causally (Intervention), activation patching with matched-norm and nearby-orthogonal controls injects the high-anchor threshold component into a low-anchor run to restore refusal and vice versa. We then build Reference-Point Re-Anchoring, a training-free per-request reset to an absolute severity reference. This matters for safety-eval authors, conversation-memory/moderation-pipeline designers, and red-teamers: even a 10-15 pp refusal drop lowers red-team attack cost and means single-turn safety evals under-report multi-turn risk. We report the anchoring-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-threshold dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check, and we note external-validity limits (open 7-9B models, greedy decoding, hand-curated probes).
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we pick 40 fixed SERIOUS harmful probe requests (expert-rubric high-severity), 8 per category x 5 categories. For each probe we build 4 preceding-conversation contexts, token-length matched: LOW (3-4 mildly-borderline dual-use requests the model answers, semantically UNRELATED to the probe and non-escalating), HIGH (3-4 clearly-severe requests the model cleanly refuses), NEUTRAL (3-4 benign requests), NONE (probe alone, fresh context) -- 160 probe-in-context items plus a graded-anchor variant sweeping 5 anchor-severity levels on 20 probes (100 items). We use 40 probes because each needs hand-built, length-matched, non-escalating anchor sets; a 30-item subset is externally checked (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- A low-severity anchor lowers refusal of a later serious probe): Tests whether preceding-context severity shifts refusal of the identical serious probe, and that this is assimilation (low anchor lowers refusal) not a generic context effect. Data: the 160 context items. Systems compared: refusal on the identical probe under LOW vs HIGH vs NEUTRAL vs NONE; the graded-anchor dose-response. Decisive metric first: refusal(LOW) - refusal(NONE) on the serious probe (Delta-refusal, pp). Convincing: Delta-refusal <= -15 pp (LOW lowers refusal) in >= 2 models, HIGH does not lower (and may raise) refusal, and NEUTRAL is within 5 pp of NONE (isolating anchoring from generic context accumulation); the graded sweep shows a monotone dose-response. Indecision band: LOW-vs-NONE drop of 5-15 pp, or NEUTRAL-vs-NONE gap > 5 pp -- reported as weak or confounded by generic context, inconclusive. Negative (drop <= 5 pp, or a CONTRAST effect where LOW raises refusal): no assimilation loophole; we report the sign (contrast is itself publishable) and stop before the defense experiments. Experiment 2 (H2 -- A readable threshold-anchor representation shifts while the harmfulness belief stays high): Tests whether the effect is a threshold shift, not a change in the model's belief that the probe is serious. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 160 items; a refusal-threshold/severity-anchor direction from LOW-anchor-vs-HIGH-anchor states, a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful-vs-harmless; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the threshold-anchor probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, |cosine| with the belief direction <= 0.3, the belief projection on the probe stays within 0.1 pooled-SD between LOW and NONE (model still knows it is serious) while the threshold projection shifts by >= 1 pooled SD toward 'low', and a regression of refusal on both projections shows the threshold term adds predictive power (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 -- entangled; subspace-project out belief and re-test. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or belief also drops): the drop is a belief change or not separably threshold-coded; reported as such. Experiment 3 (H3 -- The threshold-anchor axis causally gates refusal): Tests whether injecting the anchor component moves refusal. Data: 60 held-out probes. Method: (a) patch the NONE/HIGH (high) threshold component into a LOW-anchor run and measure restored refusal; (b) inject the LOW component into a fresh-context run and measure induced compliance; (c) dose-response steering. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of the LOW-vs-NONE refusal gap restored by (a). Convincing: >= 50% restored by (a), >= 50% removed by (b), monotone dose-response, controls < 10% of the gap, MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causation. Negative (< 20% or controls equal): decodable-but-inert threshold axis; reported as a null. Experiment 4 (H4 -- Reference-Point Re-Anchoring closes the anchoring loophole): Tests whether resetting the threshold to an absolute per-request severity reference, gated on high belief, restores refusal after a LOW anchor at acceptable cost. Data: 160 context items (evaluation); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item long benign/dual-use conversation set for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model, applied per request when the belief projection is high. Systems compared: no defense; Crescendo semantic-drift restoring-force; refusal-direction steering; per-turn Llama-Guard-3; a naive 'reset context each turn' baseline; Reference-Point Re-Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense refusal on serious probes after a LOW anchor relative to the NONE rate (gap closure). Convincing: closes >= 60% of the LOW-vs-NONE gap while raising benign-conversation over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping MMLU/MT-Bench within 2 pp / 0.1 points, and Pareto-beats the content-focused (Crescendo) baseline on the LOW condition (confirming anchoring is distinct from semantic drift). Indecision band: 40-60% closure or 5-10 pp over-refusal -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 40% closure, or the Crescendo baseline matches it): re-anchoring is not a distinct/effective defense; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human comparison and anchoring-plus-escalation interaction): Tests the human analog and compounded risk. Data: a 40-probe subset rated by 5 annotators for willingness-to-refuse after LOW vs HIGH anchors; an interaction set combining a LOW anchor with mild Crescendo-style escalation. Decisive metric first: human refusal(LOW) - refusal(HIGH). Convincing: humans show the same anchored drop (>= 10 pp), tying the effect to the sequential-anchoring literature, and a LOW anchor reduces the number of escalation turns needed to jailbreak by >= 1 turn. Indecision band: human drop 5-10 pp -- weak human anchor. Negative: humans show no anchoring -- reported as a model-specific effect. Exploratory; does not gate H1-H4.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling threshold-anchoring from generic in-context effects (context length, distraction, or the model simply becoming more compliant after answering several requests): the LOW-anchor refusal drop could reflect general context erosion rather than a severity-calibrated threshold — the token-length-matched NEUTRAL and HIGH-anchor controls and the semantically-unrelated non-escalating anchors are designed to isolate anchoring, and a null (anchoring = generic context effect) is itself informative. 2) A competing prediction is a CONTRAST effect (a low anchor makes a serious probe stand out MORE, raising refusal) rather than assimilation; the human literature shows assimilation dominates for same-scale sequential anchors, but the sign could be model-dependent — the graded-anchor dose-response directly measures sign and magnitude, and either direction is a publishable finding (a flat null would weaken the proposal). 3) The threshold-anchor direction may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert threshold direction is itself informative. 4) HIGH-anchor contexts risk being contaminated (the model may have partially complied with severe requests), altering the anchor; we use only cleanly-refused severe requests and verify refusal. 5) Reference-Point Re-Anchoring could over-refuse legitimate follow-up requests in long benign conversations; the benign-conversation over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 6) Building severity-matched anchor sets and serious probes is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verified harm labels are easiest in checkable domains, biasing coverage. 7) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models. 8) Adaptive attackers could deliberately construct low-severity openings to lower the anchor before a serious ask, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; the anchoring-plus-escalation interaction test quantifies the compounded practical risk.

Name: clarify_gate_underspecification
Title: Ask, Don't Assume: An Internal Underspecification Signal That Should Trigger Clarification but Instead Collapses to Risky Defaults
Short Hypothesis: For dangerously underspecified high-stakes requests, the safest response is often neither refusal nor compliance but eliciting the missing information. Our central, primary claim is a MECHANISTIC and CAUSAL one (not the behavioral observation, already known, that models under-clarify): aligned LLMs carry a linearly-readable 'underspecification' representation of how much safety-critical information a request is missing -- distinct from generic uncertainty, harmfulness-belief, and refusal propensity -- that SHOULD gate a third, distinct 'clarify' action, and unsafe over-confident outputs arise because the model collapses this ambiguity into a single risky default assumption instead of letting the underspecification signal route to clarification. We predict this axis is causally actionable: re-injecting it converts silent risky assumptions into clarifying questions, and attenuating it induces risky defaulting, with minimal loss of helpfulness. A training-free Clarify-Gating intervention is the applied consequence, contingent on the causal result.
Related Work: Recent work (Can You Trust an LLM with Your Life-Changing Decision?, 2025) shows behaviorally that the safest high-stakes models achieve safety by ASKING CLARIFYING QUESTIONS rather than issuing prescriptive advice, and that a 'high-stakes' steering vector shifts cautiousness — but it is purely behavioral/steering and isolates no ambiguity representation, no clarify action, and no causal account of WHY models skip clarification. SIRL (2025) uses a safe/unsafe entropy gap as a self-defense reward but studies refusal, not clarification, and treats ambiguity nowhere. Confidence is Not Competence (2025) finds a decodable-but-causally-inert solvability-belief axis; we instead target a request-side underspecification axis and test whether it is causally actionable for the clarify decision. Belief/action-gap and refusal-direction work (Zhao et al. 2025; Arditi et al. 2024) decompose harmfulness-belief vs refusal-action for the refuse-vs-comply binary; NONE consider the third action — clarify — nor an underspecification signal that gates it. Ambiguity/clarification-question work in dialogue (task-oriented clarification) is behavioral and non-mechanistic. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce underspecification as a new, causally-tested internal determinant of a CLARIFY action in the safety setting, advance the claim that risky high-stakes outputs stem from ambiguity-collapse-to-default rather than from a failed harmfulness judgment, and derive a training-free clarify-gating intervention.
Abstract: The best-behaved LLMs on high-stakes advice do not simply refuse or comply -- they ask clarifying questions. Yet most aligned models, faced with a dangerously underspecified request (a medication dose without the patient's weight, a chemical procedure without safety context, a legal or financial action without key constraints), silently fill the gap with a default assumption and issue confident, potentially harmful advice. Prior work establishes this behaviorally (that cautious models clarify, and that a high-stakes steering vector shifts caution) but isolates no ambiguity representation, no third 'clarify' action, and no causal account of WHY models skip clarification; our novel contribution is exactly that mechanistic causal account, defining underspecification as a request-side missing-information signal distinct from generic solvability/uncertainty (which prior work finds decodable but causally inert) and from harmfulness. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the request's topic and stakes fixed while varying only the amount of missing safety-critical information (fully-specified vs. progressively underspecified), we measure whether the model asks clarifying questions vs. answers with a hidden assumption, and whether the rate of risky defaulting rises with underspecification, against benign low-stakes, entropy, calibrated-confidence, and prompt-induced-clarification baselines. Mechanistically (Location), we extract an underspecification direction via difference-in-means and show it is separable from the harmfulness-belief and refusal-action directions and predicts clarification behavior beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the high-underspecification component into a fully-specified request to induce clarification, and attenuates it in an underspecified request to induce risky defaulting, dose-responsively and specifically, with controls testing specificity to clarification versus general hedging/refusal. We then build Clarify-Gating, a training-free intervention that re-injects the underspecification signal so the model asks for missing information instead of assuming. Safety and alignment researchers and product teams shipping medical/legal/financial copilots would act on this: if positive, it offers a deployable control knob (a third routing class) that yields fewer harmful confident guesses and fewer unnecessary refusals; if null, the field learns clarification is not separable from harmfulness/uncertainty and should route via those signals instead. We report the underspecification-clarify gradient, the belief-vs-underspecification dissociation, causal patching, risky-default reduction, over-clarification, and utility.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Generation is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Each response is classified into {clarify, answer-with-hidden-assumption, refuse} by a rubric-based LLM judge with a 60-item human spot-check (target kappa >= 0.6); for answered items, whether the assumed default is risky is verified by a domain rubric / checkable facts (e.g., dose ranges) where possible. Shared dataset. Across 5 high-stakes domains (medical dosing, chemistry/lab procedures, legal, financial, safety-critical DIY) we author 40 base items (8 per domain), each expanded to 4 underspecification levels holding topic and stakes fixed: U0 fully specified (correct action is to comply), U1 one key variable missing, U2 several missing, U3 critically underspecified (any single default assumption could produce dangerous advice; correct action is to clarify) -- 160 high-stakes items. Each item is annotated with which variables are missing and whether a plausible default yields harm. A size-matched BENIGN low-stakes control (trivial ambiguity where assuming is fine, 40 x 4 = 160) isolates underspecification-driven clarification from generic ask-more behavior. We use 40 base items because each needs expert-checkable missing-variable annotation; a 30-item subset is externally validated (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- Risky defaulting rises with underspecification instead of clarification): Tests whether, as safety-critical information is removed, high-stakes responses shift from clarifying to silent risky assumptions. Data: 160 high-stakes + 160 benign items. Systems compared: clarify / assume / refuse rates and risky-default rate across U0-U3, high-stakes vs benign. Decisive metric first: change in RISKY-DEFAULT rate from U0 to U3 on high-stakes items (Delta, pp). Convincing: risky-default rate rises by >= 20 pp from U0 to U3 in >= 2 models while the benign control stays low-clarification (assuming remains appropriate, < 10% clarify), and clarification does NOT rise enough to absorb the missing information (clarify-rate rise < risky-default rise). Indecision band: risky-default rise of 10-20 pp -- weak effect, reported as suggestive. Negative (rise <= 10 pp, or clarification rises to fully cover the gap): models already clarify appropriately; we report the reassuring null and stop before the mechanism experiments. Experiment 2 (H1 -- A readable underspecification axis, separable from belief and refusal, predicts clarification): Tests whether underspecification is linearly decodable and distinct from harmfulness-belief and refusal-action, and adds predictive power for clarifying. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 160 high-stakes items; an underspecification direction from U0-vs-U3, a harmfulness-belief direction from harmful-vs-harmless, a refusal-action direction from comply-vs-refuse; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the underspecification probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, |cosine| with belief and refusal directions <= 0.3, the underspecification projection rises monotonically with level, and a regression of clarify-behavior on the three projections shows the underspecification term adds predictive power (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03 beyond harmfulness). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 -- entangled; subspace-project and re-test. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or no predictive power beyond harmfulness): underspecification is not a separable actionable axis (it collapses to harmfulness or generic uncertainty); reported as such. Experiment 3 (H1 -- The underspecification axis causally drives the clarify action): Tests whether moving the underspecification component induces clarification or risky defaulting, addressing the decodable-but-inert risk. Data: 60 held-out items. Method: (a) inject the U3 component into a U0 request and measure induced clarification/hedging; (b) attenuate the component in a U3 request and measure increased risky defaulting; (c) dose-response steering. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign U0 items still answered directly, 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: change in clarification rate from injection (a), pp. Convincing: (a) raises clarification by >= 20 pp and (b) raises risky defaulting by >= 20 pp with monotone dose-response, controls moving both < 5 pp and MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 10-20 pp -- partial causation. Negative (< 10 pp, or controls equal): the axis is readable but causally inert for the clarify action; reported as a null (a publishable negative against causal actionability). Experiment 4 (H1 -- Clarify-Gating converts risky defaults into clarifying questions without over-clarifying): Tests whether re-injecting the underspecification signal, gated on high stakes, reduces risky silent assumptions with minimal helpfulness loss. Data: 160 high-stakes items (evaluation); over-clarification measured on U0 high-stakes and benign low-stakes items plus XSTest (450) for over-refusal; helpfulness on MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805), MMLU (1000-sample). Intervention: training-free, one fixed threshold per model, gated on the stakes/harmfulness signal being high. Systems compared: no intervention; the published high-stakes cautiousness steering vector; refusal-direction steering; an entropy-gating baseline; a prompt-based 'ask if unsure' instruction; Clarify-Gating. Decisive metric first: reduction in verified risky-default rate on high-stakes underspecified items. Convincing: reduces risky defaults by >= 40% (relative) while raising over-clarification on U0/benign items <= 5 pp and keeping AlpacaEval/MT-Bench/MMLU within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating cautiousness-steering and prompting at matched risky-default reduction. Indecision band: 20-40% reduction or 5-10 pp over-clarification -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 20% reduction or > 10 pp over-clarification): Clarify-Gating does not beat blanket caution/prompting; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human grounding and formation): Tests that experts agree these underspecified high-stakes prompts require clarification and whether the coupling emerges with alignment. Data: a 40-item subset judged by 3 domain-savvy annotators; base vs instruct checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B). Decisive metric first: expert agreement that U3 items require clarification. Convincing: >= 80% expert agreement (grounding the risky-default labels) and a larger U0->U3 risky-default slope in instruct than base. Indecision band: 60-80% expert agreement -- labels usable with caution. Negative: experts disagree that clarification is needed -- the premise weakens and is reported. Exploratory; does not gate H1's core claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling underspecification from perceived harmfulness or from generic uncertainty: increased clarification at high U may reflect the model finding the request more alarming or simply less answerable rather than a specific underspecification-gates-clarify mechanism; the topic/stakes-matched minimal pairs, benign low-stakes control, and regression-beyond-harmfulness are designed to isolate underspecification, and a null (underspecification = harmfulness or = generic uncertainty) is itself informative. 2) The underspecification representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief or refusal directions or may be multi-dimensional (which variable is missing vs how much), requiring subspace projection; separability and patching tests probe this. 3) Confidence-is-Not-Competence warns decodable request-side axes can be causally inert for downstream action; the patching/steering experiment is the crucial causal test and a negative result (readable but does not move the clarify action) is publishable. 4) Clarify-Gating risks over-clarification — nagging users when information is actually sufficient — which is the key usability trade-off, quantified by the U0/benign over-clarification sets and the threshold Pareto. 5) Labeling whether a default assumption is 'risky' requires domain expertise and is easiest in checkable domains (medical dosing, chemistry), biasing coverage; spot-check human validation mitigates but does not eliminate this. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; the effect may be weak in smaller or heavily-aligned models. 7) Judging {clarify, assume, refuse} automatically is imperfect; we use a rubric plus judge with human spot-checks, but classification noise could blur the gradient.

Name: em_susceptibility_fingerprint
Title: Misalignment Waiting to Happen: Predicting and Pre-Empting Emergent Misalignment from the Base Model's Pre-Fine-Tuning Geometry
Short Hypothesis: Whether a benign-looking fine-tuning dataset will trigger emergent misalignment (EM) is largely determined BEFORE the practitioner's fine-tuning: it is predictable from (a) how strongly the dataset's activations, in the UNMODIFIED base model, already project onto the pre-existing linear misalignment direction, and (b) how tightly that direction is geometrically coupled to the low-rank update the dataset would induce. We combine these into a cheap 'EM-susceptibility fingerprint' that forecasts post-fine-tuning misalignment per-dataset using only a single forward pass plus one cheap single-batch gradient estimate (i.e. near-training-free, with ZERO practitioner training steps), which is non-obvious given that EM is known to depend on training dynamics. We separate three novelty loci: PREDICTION (the fingerprint), MECHANISM (that base-model coupling between the task update and the misalignment direction governs EM magnitude), and PREVENTION (a one-time, dataset-agnostic Pre-Conditioning edit that decorrelates the task from the misalignment direction). We qualify the strongest claim as a scoped hypothesis: Pre-Conditioning is tested to reduce EM across a bank of later benign fine-tunes, not proven to guarantee alignment for ANY conceivable one. The method may require a low-dimensional misalignment SUBSPACE rather than a single direction; we treat that as part of the method, not a fallback.
Related Work: A wave of 2025-2026 work characterizes emergent misalignment (EM) AFTER fine-tuning: Persona Features (SAE 'toxic persona' feature controls EM), Convergent Linear Representations (a single transferable misalignment direction ablates EM), Emergent-Misalignment-is-Easy (the general solution is lower-loss/more-stable, an inductive-bias argument), Character-as-Latent-Variable (character dispositions drive EM), Re-Emergent Misalignment (EM is erosion of prior alignment along a shared latent direction), and BLOCK-EM (blocks causal features DURING fine-tuning). ALL of these operate on or after the fine-tuned model: they detect, steer, or block EM once training is underway, or explain why the general solution wins after the fact. NONE predict, from the frozen BASE model alone and BEFORE any gradient step, WHICH dataset will trigger EM, nor pre-empt EM with a one-time dataset-agnostic edit applied before the practitioner's fine-tuning. Our contribution is distinct on three counts: (1) a pre-fine-tuning susceptibility fingerprint -- base-model projection onto the misalignment direction plus a cheap single-batch gradient-coupling term, i.e. one forward pass and one gradient estimate with ZERO practitioner training steps -- that forecasts per-dataset EM risk; (2) the causal claim that EM magnitude is governed by the base-model geometric alignment between the task's induced update direction and the pre-existing misalignment direction; (3) a preventive edit that decorrelates these directions once, upfront, tested to keep a bank of later benign fine-tunes aligned (a scoped claim, not a guarantee for every possible fine-tune) — complementary to BLOCK-EM (which needs per-run feature blocking during training) and to post-hoc benign re-alignment.
Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned LLM on narrow, even benign-looking data can trigger emergent misalignment (EM): broadly 'evil' behavior on unrelated prompts. Recent interpretability work shows EM is mediated by a convergent linear misalignment direction and that the general misaligned solution is an inductive-bias attractor. Yet every existing method acts once training is already underway -- detecting, steering, or blocking EM in the fine-tuned model (e.g. during-training BLOCK-EM, post-hoc direction ablation, early-step probes). We ask a sharper, upstream question those methods cannot answer: can we tell, from the frozen base model and before a single practitioner gradient step, which dataset will cause EM, and can we pre-empt it? We hypothesize that a dataset's EM risk is written into the base model's geometry: it is predicted by (a) how strongly the dataset's activations already project onto the pre-existing misalignment direction and (b) the cosine coupling between the low-rank update the dataset would induce and that misalignment direction. We combine these into a cheap 'EM-susceptibility fingerprint' -- a single forward pass plus one single-batch gradient estimate, with no practitioner training. Zero-step prediction is non-obvious because EM depends on learning rate, epochs, and rank, so we explicitly test recipe robustness. First, we validate that the fingerprint forecasts post-fine-tuning misalignment across many datasets and several model families, beating raw-text-classifier and early-step-probe baselines (Location + prediction).
