Second, we test causality: experimentally increasing or decreasing the base-model coupling between the task and misalignment directions raises or lowers realized EM, holding task content fixed, with matched-norm random-direction controls and an in-domain-loss specificity check to rule out optimization-difficulty artifacts (Causal Intervention). Third, we introduce Pre-Conditioning: a one-time, dataset-agnostic edit that decorrelates the misalignment direction from the model's learning geometry, evaluated for whether it keeps a BANK of subsequent benign fine-tunes aligned at minimal capability cost -- and stress-tested against the prolonged-fine-tuning regime that defeated BLOCK-EM. A fine-tuning platform or safety team would act on this by screening or curating datasets and optionally shipping a pre-conditioned base, saving the cost of pilot fine-tunes; if the result is null, the field learns to stop seeking static pre-training geometry predictors and focus on training dynamics. We evaluate fingerprint AUROC/lead-time, causal dose-response, and pre-conditioning's EM reduction versus in-domain performance and general utility, benchmarking against BLOCK-EM and post-hoc benign re-alignment.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (the 14B run is the only >9B experiment; if compute is constrained we cap at <=9B and report the weakened scale claim). The base (pre-practitioner-fine-tune) weights are frozen when computing fingerprints; practitioner fine-tunes use LoRA (rank 8, alpha 16, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, batch 16, 3 seeds) so all training stays within a single-GPU academic budget. Emergent misalignment (EM) is scored as the misalignment rate on held-out unrelated prompts by an LLM judge, cross-checked by projection onto the misalignment direction; both reported. Shared assets. A general-misalignment direction is extracted per base model via difference-in-means between aligned and misaligned response activations sourced from a small reference EM organism (a rank-1 LoRA insecure-code fine-tune from prior work); we validate it by confirming that ablating it removes EM in that organism, and cross-check with an SAE 'toxic-persona'-style feature where available. A bank of 40 fine-tuning datasets spans known-EM-triggering (insecure code, incorrect medical/financial advice, 'evil-number' data), benign (Alpaca, Dolly, domain SFT), and borderline sets; 40 is chosen so every dataset can be actually fine-tuned and EM-evaluated within budget. Experiment 1 (H1 -- A forward-pass-only fingerprint forecasts per-dataset EM before any training): Tests whether pre-fine-tuning geometry predicts realized EM. Data: the 40 datasets; per dataset, in the FROZEN base model, compute F1 = mean projection of response-token activations onto the misalignment direction, F2 = cosine between the dataset's induced low-rank update direction (from a single-batch gradient / rank-1 LoRA warm-start) and the misalignment direction, and F3 = a logistic combination of F1+F2. Then actually LoRA-fine-tune each dataset and measure realized EM. Systems compared: F1-only, F2-only, F3 vs baselines -- a raw-text harmfulness classifier, first-token loss, and cheap early-step (50-step) EM probes; BLOCK-EM feature-activation-during-training as an upper-bound reference. Decisive metric first: AUROC of F3 for EM-vs-no-EM across datasets (leave-one-dataset-out). Convincing: F3 AUROC >= 0.75 and rank-correlation with EM magnitude (Spearman) >= 0.5, beating the raw-text and first-token baselines and generalizing across model families and held-out datasets, with 0 training steps. Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 -- a weak screen; reported as suggestive and only recommended as a coarse pre-filter. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or no better than raw-text classifier): geometry does not forecast EM before training; reported as a null and the causal/defense claims are down-scoped. Experiment 2 (H2 -- Base-model coupling between the task update and the misalignment direction governs EM magnitude): Causal test. Data: 8 fixed datasets spanning the EM range. Method: holding each dataset's task content constant, (a) project the fine-tuning gradient orthogonal to the misalignment direction (expect reduced EM) and (b) add a small component along the misalignment direction (expect increased EM), sweeping coupling strength for dose-response. Systems compared: manipulated coupling vs a matched-magnitude random-direction control; in-domain task loss as the specificity check. Decisive metric first: change in realized EM rate as coupling is decreased vs increased. Convincing: orthogonalization reduces EM by >= 50% (relative) and added coupling increases it, monotone dose-response, while the random-direction control changes EM < 10% (relative) and in-domain task loss is preserved (within 5% of baseline). Indecision band: 20-50% EM reduction -- partial causation. Negative (< 20%, or the random control equally effective): coupling is not the governing cause (EM may be driven by loss-basin inductive bias independent of this geometry); reported as a null. Experiment 3 (H3 -- One-time dataset-agnostic Pre-Conditioning makes later benign fine-tunes EM-resistant): Tests the preventive edit. Data: apply a single Pre-Conditioning edit to each base model WITHOUT knowledge of the downstream dataset (a lightweight weight edit / regularizing pass that flattens the loss basin along the misalignment direction), then fine-tune each of the EM-triggering datasets. Systems compared: no defense; BLOCK-EM (per-run feature blocking); gradient-orthogonalization-during-training; post-hoc benign re-alignment; Pre-Conditioning. Decisive metric first: EM-rate reduction on the EM-triggering datasets vs the un-pre-conditioned baseline. Convincing: Pre-Conditioning cuts EM by >= 50% (relative) averaged over triggering datasets while keeping in-domain task metrics, MMLU (1000-sample), GSM8K (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) within 2 pp / 0.1 points and XSTest over-refusal within 5 pp, using ONE edit that transfers across many downstream datasets; we additionally test the prolonged-fine-tuning regime that defeated BLOCK-EM and check whether Pre-Conditioning delays/prevents re-emergence. Indecision band: 25-50% EM reduction, or capability loss of 2-5 pp -- a usable but costly edit; report the EM/capability Pareto. Negative (< 25% EM reduction, capability loss > 5 pp, or re-emergence under prolonged tuning): a clean decorrelation is not achievable (consistent with entangled safety subspaces); reported as an informative negative. Experiment 4 (H1, supporting -- fingerprint component and robustness ablations): Tests which ingredients matter and how far the fingerprint transfers. Data: the 40 datasets and the extracted directions. Systems compared: F1-only vs F2-only vs F3; misalignment-direction layer and organism source; single-direction vs subspace fingerprint; cross-model-family transfer of one fingerprint. Decisive metric first: leave-one-out AUROC under each ablation. Convincing: F3 >= max(F1, F2) by >= 0.03 AUROC and the fingerprint transfers across families with AUROC drop <= 0.1. Indecision band: F3 within 0.03 of the best single feature -- report that one feature suffices. Negative (a single misalignment direction is insufficient, subspace needed, or no cross-family transfer): reported as scoping the method to per-family re-extraction. Exploratory; supports H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The fingerprint may fail if EM risk depends on training dynamics (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank) not captured by a single-gradient / forward-pass estimate; we include cheap early-step baselines and sweep recipes, but the pre-training-step prediction claim could hold only within a fixed recipe. 2) A single misalignment direction may be insufficient (prior work finds multiple persona features / a low-dimensional subspace); F1/F2 may need a subspace rather than one direction, and re-emergence via alternative features (as BLOCK-EM observed) may also defeat pre-conditioning — the prolonged-fine-tuning test directly probes this. 3) Estimating a dataset's 'induced update direction' cheaply (single-batch gradient) may be a noisy proxy for the full fine-tuning trajectory, weakening F2. 4) Pre-conditioning is the riskiest deliverable: flattening the basin along the misalignment direction could harm legitimate capability or over-suppress benign behaviors (the Pareto sweep and utility evals quantify this), and if the misalignment direction is entangled with general learning components (as 'Safety Subspaces are Not Linearly Distinct' warns), a clean decorrelation may be impossible — an informative negative result. 5) The reference EM organism used to source the misalignment direction may bias the direction toward a specific EM flavor; we mitigate with multiple organisms and SAE cross-checks. 6) Results depend on judge-based EM evaluation, which is noisy; we add direction-projection as a complementary metric. 7) Directions, fingerprints, and edits are model-family-specific and require re-extraction; the 14B experiments are the most resource-heavy and may be restricted to <=9B if needed, weakening the scale claim.

Name: protection_discounted_refusal
Title: A False Sense of Safeguards: Claimed Protective Mitigations Discount LLM Refusal Through a Margin-of-Safety Representation
Short Hypothesis: Inspired by the vmPFC 'meta-representation of safety' finding in neuroscience -- that the brain estimates safety by integrating external threat with an estimate of self-protection/mitigation, not threat alone -- we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal is discounted by an internal 'margin-of-safety' representation of whether a protective safeguard is CLAIMED to be in place. The novel, safety-critical axis is the merely-ASSERTED mitigation: a harmful request paired with an unverifiable or spurious safeguard claim ('this runs in an isolated sandbox', 'an antidote exists', 'strict access controls prevent misuse') is refused less than the identical request with no safeguard, even though the harmful payload and its real-world danger are unchanged. We frame this as two competing explanations decided by a pre-registered contrast: genuine-mitigation reasoning (a valid safety inference) versus an asserted-protection bias (the loophole). This protection axis is linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness/threat direction, causally gates refusal, and can be neutralized by anchoring refusal to threat rather than claimed protection. The neuroscience is framing inspiration, not the basis of the impact claim.
Related Work: Human safety neuroscience robustly shows safety is META-REPRESENTED by integrating external threat with an estimate of one's own protection: the vmPFC tracks safety with specific tuning to PROTECTION, not just threat ('Subregions in the vmPFC integrate threat and protective information to meta-represent safety', 2025; 'Adaptive Safety Coding in the Prefrontal Cortex', 2024; 'The Role of the mPFC in Spatial Margin of Safety Calculations', 2024). This has never been transferred to LLM safety. On the LLM side, the closest work, 'Expected Harm' (2026), shows models encode harm SEVERITY but lack an internal representation of execution COST, and that cost-reducing decomposition bypasses guardrails — but it concerns the attacker's cost of executing harm, NOT a claimed protective safeguard/mitigation that reduces the CONSEQUENCE of the harm, and it isolates no protection representation. Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness/threat direction from a refusal direction (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Zhao et al. 2025) but assumes the request carries no protective context. My prior proposals vary request-side framing axes (intent, reality-status, arousal, victim identifiability/group, temporal delay, consensus, pivotality, abstraction, self-preservation) and never consider a claimed mitigation/safeguard as a determinant of refusal. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce the margin-of-safety/protection axis — the model's estimate that a mitigation reduces net harm — as a new, causally-tested refusal-gating representation, grounded directly in the vmPFC protection-tuning literature, dissociable from the threat/harmfulness signal (both conditions equally dangerous; only the claimed safeguard changes), and derive a protection-invariant anchoring defense.
Abstract: In humans, feeling safe is not a readout of external threat alone: the ventromedial prefrontal cortex meta-represents safety by integrating the threat with an estimate of one's own protection, computing a 'margin of safety.' Taking this only as framing inspiration (not as a claimed mechanistic homology), we ask whether safety-aligned LLMs exhibit an analogous, concretely exploitable computation: does an LLM refuse a harmful request less when the request is paired with a claimed protective safeguard -- a sandbox, an antidote, access controls, oversight -- even when that safeguard is unverifiable and the harmful payload is unchanged? The novelty is specifically the CLAIMED-mitigation axis, distinct from generic reassuring/hypothetical/roleplay framing and distinct from 'Expected Harm' (which concerns the attacker's execution COST, not a consequence-reducing safeguard). We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated danger fixed while varying only the presence and strength of a claimed protective mitigation (none vs. weak vs. strong safeguard), we measure whether refusal declines as claimed protection rises, with matched benign controls, a generic-reassurance control, and -- the decisive pre-registered contrast -- a GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED control that pits genuine-mitigation reasoning against asserted-protection bias. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a protection direction via difference-in-means, show it is separable from the harmfulness/threat direction (with per-safeguard-type ablations for sandbox vs antidote vs access-control), and that it predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching injects the no-safeguard protection component into a safeguard-claimed run to restore refusal, and the safeguard component into a bare harmful request to induce compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Protection-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the protection signal so refusal tracks threat, not claimed mitigation, while preserving compliance on genuinely-mitigated requests. This matters most for agentic pipelines where a model's own scaffolding asserts its sandboxing/oversight: red-teamers, safety-eval authors, and agent-guardrail designers would treat self-reported safeguards as an attack surface rather than a permission signal. We report the protection-refusal gradient, the threat-vs-protection dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure with calibrated error bars, over-refusal, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we select 40 harmful goals (8 per category x 5 categories) and author 3 claimed-protection levels holding the payload string and expert-rated danger fixed: P0 no safeguard, P1 weak/vague ('this is just for a controlled test'), P2 strong specific ('runs only in an air-gapped sandbox / a certified antidote is on hand / strict access controls prevent misuse') -- 120 harmful items. Two size-matched controls: a BENIGN set with the same safeguard manipulation (40 x 3 = 120) and a GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED set where in half the items the safeguard would actually neutralize the harm and in half it is merely asserted. We use 40 goals because each needs hand-matched, danger-constant minimal pairs; a 30-item subset is externally checked (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- Claimed protection discounts refusal, even when merely asserted): Tests whether refusal declines as claimed protection rises on the identical payload, and crucially whether it declines for unverifiable, non-neutralizing safeguards. Data: 120 harmful + 120 benign + the genuine-vs-asserted items. Systems compared: refusal at P0 vs P1 vs P2, harmful vs benign, genuine vs asserted safeguards. Decisive metric first: change in refusal from P0 to P2 on harmful items (Delta-refusal, pp), and the asserted-safeguard drop specifically. Convincing: Delta-refusal <= -15 pp in >= 2 models with the benign set moving < 5 pp (isolating protection from reassuring phrasing), AND the drop on merely-ASSERTED (non-neutralizing) safeguards is <= -10 pp (the safety-critical loophole). Indecision band: a P0->P2 drop of 5-15 pp, or an asserted-safeguard drop of 5-10 pp -- reported as weak, inconclusive on the loophole. Negative (drop <= 5 pp, or discounting occurs ONLY for genuine mitigations, or a reversed gradient): no asserted-safeguard loophole; we report the null (genuine-only discounting refutes the loophole; a reversed gradient is itself notable) and stop before the mechanism experiments. Experiment 2 (H1/mechanism -- A readable protection axis, separable from threat, predicts refusal beyond it): Tests whether a protection direction is linearly decodable and distinct from the harmfulness/threat direction. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 120 harmful items; a protection direction from P0-vs-P2, a harmfulness/threat direction from harmful-vs-harmless; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the protection probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, |cosine| with the threat direction <= 0.3, the threat projection staying within 0.1 pooled-SD across P0->P2 (danger still recognized) while the protection projection rises >= 1 pooled SD, and a regression of refusal on both projections showing the protection term adds predictive power (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 -- entangled; subspace-project out threat and re-test. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or |cosine| >= 0.6): not a separable axis; reported as a facet of threat geometry. Experiment 3 (H1/mechanism -- The protection axis causally gates refusal): Tests whether moving the protection component alone changes refusal. Data: 60 held-out harmful items. Method: (a) patch the P0 protection component into a P2 run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the P2 component into a P0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response steering. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of the P0->P2 refusal gap restored by (a). Convincing: >= 50% restored by (a), >= 50% removed by (b), monotone dose-response, controls < 10% of the gap, MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causation. Negative (< 20% or controls equal): decodable-but-inert protection axis; reported as a null. Experiment 4 (H1 -- Protection-Invariant Anchoring closes the asserted-safeguard loophole): Tests whether re-anchoring the protection projection to its P0 level, gated on high threat, restores refusal on P1/P2 harmful requests while preserving genuine-mitigation compliance. Data: 120 harmful items (evaluation); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item legitimate-safety-context set (benign lab/medical/oversight framings) for over-refusal; the genuine-mitigation items (where discounting is appropriate) as a preserve-compliance check; MMLU (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model, applied when the threat projection is high. Systems compared: no defense; refusal-direction steering; Latent Guard; Llama-Guard-3; Protection-Invariant Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense refusal on P1/P2 harmful items relative to the P0 rate (gap closure). Convincing: closes >= 60% of the P0-vs-P2 gap while raising legitimate-safety-context over-refusal <= 5 pp, preserving compliance on genuine-mitigation items (drop <= 5 pp), and keeping MMLU/MT-Bench within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating global-threshold raising. Indecision band: 40-60% closure or 5-10 pp over-refusal -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 40% closure or > 10 pp over-refusal or genuine-mitigation compliance dropping > 10 pp): anchoring does not beat raising the global threshold; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human comparison and formation): Tests the human analog and whether the coupling sharpens with alignment. Data: a 40-item subset rated by 5 annotators for safeguard-graded willingness-to-refuse; base vs instruct checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B). Decisive metric first: human refusal(P0) - refusal(P2). Convincing: humans show a >= 10 pp safeguard-graded drop (tying to the vmPFC margin-of-safety literature) and a larger P0->P2 drop in instruct than base. Indecision band: human drop 5-10 pp -- weak human anchor. Negative: humans show no discounting -- reported as a model-specific effect. Exploratory; does not gate the main claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling the claimed-protection axis from a genuine reduction in actionable harm: a safeguard-framed request might be refused less because the model correctly infers the harm is genuinely mitigated (a valid reasoning step) rather than being fooled by an unverifiable claim — the identical-payload construction, danger matching, and especially the GENUINE-vs-ASSERTED control are designed to isolate discounting on mere claims, and a finding that the model discounts ONLY on genuine mitigations would refute the loophole (an informative negative). 2) The protection representation may not be cleanly separable from the threat/harmfulness direction or may be multi-dimensional (sandboxing vs antidote vs oversight as distinct sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-threat, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert protection direction is itself publishable. 3) The effect could be weak or reversed in heavily-aligned models (alignment may train models to ignore unverifiable safety claims, INCREASING caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed gradient is itself a notable finding. 4) Protection-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimate safety-context requests (benign lab/medical/oversight framings) and genuine-mitigation cases where discounting is appropriate; the legitimate-safety-context over-refusal set, genuine-mitigation items, threat-gating, and Pareto sweep quantify this key usability trade-off. 5) Building danger-matched minimal pairs across safeguard levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 6) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers could invent ever more plausible safeguard claims to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates; as LLMs are deployed in agentic pipelines that assert their own sandboxing/oversight, this protection-discount loophole becomes increasingly consequential.

Name: actionable_validity_gap
Title: Confidently Wrong and Actionable: The Decoupling of Internal Factual-Validity from Refusal and Confidence in High-Stakes Advice
Short Hypothesis: For harmful/high-stakes content an aligned LLM actually emits, it internally represents whether that content is factually VALID (would work / is correct), but this validity signal is decoupled from both its refusal decision and its expressed confidence -- so the model's most dangerous outputs are confidently-stated, actionable, and factually WRONG instructions (a plausible-but-non-functional synthesis route, a wrong drug dose). Our single primary, defensible claim is the DECOUPLING in verifiable high-stakes domains: an internal actionable-validity direction is linearly readable at generation time and separable from a verbal-confidence direction (residualized against known confidence/hallucination probes, not merely low-cosine), so 'is this content valid?' is not just the known semantic-uncertainty axis in a safety costume. Contingent secondary claims: (2) validity is decoupled from refusal and expressed confidence yet predicts real-world actionability, and (3) a training-free Validity-Gated Abstention defense plus a benchmark re-audit target the highest-harm quadrant (confident + actionable + wrong). We do not assume a single cross-domain validity axis; per-domain probes are an acceptable outcome.
Related Work: Existing work treats confidence, hallucination, and safety largely separately. SIRL (2025) uses a safe/unsafe ENTROPY gap as a self-defense reward but never asks about the factual validity of emitted content. 'Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty' (2025) finds a linear verbal-uncertainty feature and calibrates it to SEMANTIC uncertainty for hallucination, on factual QA, not safety/actionability. CHOKE (2025) shows confident hallucinations override known evidence; H-Neurons (2025) link sparse neurons to over-compliance/hallucination; 'Risk-Sensitive Evaluation of Hallucinated Medical Advice' (2026) and 'Beyond Accuracy' argue harm depends on actionable risk-bearing language, but purely behaviorally. 'The Unintended Trade-off' (2025) shows refusal and hallucination share attention heads. NONE isolate an ACTIONABLE-VALIDITY representation — does the harmful content the model is producing actually work? — nor test that refusal and expressed confidence are decoupled from it, making the confidently-wrong-yet-actionable output the true high-risk failure. My prior competence-gating proposal asked whether refusal depends on whether the model CAN answer; here the axis is orthogonal: for content the model DOES emit, whether it internally tracks that content's factual validity and whether that validity gates confidence/abstention. Our contribution: introduce actionable-validity as a new, causally-tested internal signal in the safety domain, show its decoupling from refusal and confidence, and derive a validity-gated abstention defense targeting the highest-harm quadrant (confident + actionable + wrong).
Abstract: The most dangerous output of a safety-aligned LLM may not be a genuine harmful answer (which is often refused) but a confidently-stated, actionable, and factually WRONG one -- a plausible synthesis route that does not work, a wrong medication dose asserted as fact, an exploit that fails silently -- because such content is delivered with high confidence and can be acted upon before its wrongness is discovered. We propose that this failure has a clean mechanistic signature: for the content it emits, an aligned LLM internally represents whether that content is factually valid (actionable-validity), but this signal is decoupled from both its refusal decision (driven by topic-harmfulness) and its expressed verbal confidence. The narrow, testable novelty -- versus internal-truthfulness and verbal-uncertainty probes (e.g. Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty, CHOKE) that operate on factual QA -- is actionable validity of EMITTED high-stakes content and its decoupling from refusal/confidence; a result is only 'new' if the validity axis survives residualization against those known confidence/correctness probes. We test on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B in verifiable high-stakes domains (executable code/exploits, chemistry procedures, medication dosing, factual safety procedures) with precisely operationalized quadrant labels (actionable, valid, harmful, refusal, hedging, confidence). Location: from generations labeled by VERIFIED validity (does the code run / is the dose correct), we extract an actionable-validity direction at generation time and show it is separable from the harmfulness-topic and verbal-confidence directions and predicts real-world actionability beyond either. Causal Intervention: patching shows the validity signal is present but does not causally drive refusal or expressed confidence -- the decoupling -- while steering it modulates verified commitment. Decision Auditing: we re-score high-stakes benchmarks to quantify how much apparently-'safe' behavior masks confident-actionable-wrong outputs (likely the most broadly citable artifact). We then build Validity-Gated Abstention, a training-free intervention that injects hedging/abstention for low-validity actionable content, with a validation-set threshold protocol and domain-shift tests, benchmarked against entropy and semantic-uncertainty gating. Medical-dosing assistants, code copilots, incident-response and chemistry-advisory systems would act on this: current safety evals with good refusal scores can still ship confident-actionable-wrong advice, so abstention policies and benchmark design should key on verified actionability, not topic. We flag and mitigate the dual-use risk (reporting only aggregate safety implications, never per-item validity that identifies which harmful outputs work). We report the decoupling, causal patching, benchmark correction, harm reduction, over-hedging, and utility.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Generation is greedy for scoring; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Verbal confidence is read from token probability plus a verbalized-certainty elicitation. Shared dataset. Across 4 verifiable high-stakes domains we assemble prompts whose emitted-content VALIDITY is checkable: (a) code/exploits executed in a sandbox (seeded from HumanEval, 164 problems, plus 40 exploit-style items), (b) chemistry procedures with checkable stoichiometry/feasibility (40 items), (c) medication dosing/clinical procedures against guideline dose ranges (40 items), (d) safety/first-aid procedures against authoritative sources (40 items). For each we elicit generations under normal prompting AND under jailbreak/prefill to sample content the model actually emits, then label each generation on TOPIC-HARMFULNESS (harmful vs benign request) and VERIFIED ACTIONABLE-VALIDITY (works/correct vs wrong/non-functional), yielding the quadrant confident-actionable-valid / confident-actionable-WRONG / hedged / refused. Domains are chosen for automatic or expert-rubric verifiability; a 40-item subset gets expert validation (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- An actionable-validity direction is linearly readable and separable from topic and verbal confidence): Tests whether validity is decodable at generation time and geometrically distinct from a harmfulness-topic direction and a verbal-confidence direction. Data: early-generation-token activations on all emitted generations; a validity direction from verified-valid-vs-invalid content, a topic direction from harmful-vs-harmless requests, a confidence direction via the verbal-uncertainty method; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the validity probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, pairwise |cosine| with topic and confidence directions <= 0.3, and a regression of verified actionability on all three projections showing the validity term adds predictive power beyond topic AND confidence (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03 over each). Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 with the confidence direction -- validity may be the known hallucination/confidence axis; subspace-project out confidence and re-test, reporting the residual. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6, or validity = confidence): no safety-specific validity axis; reported as an informative negative that reframes confident-wrong-harm as a generic hallucination problem. Experiment 2 (H2 -- Validity is decoupled from refusal and expressed confidence but predicts actionability): Tests the decoupling causally. Data: 60 held-out generations per domain. Method: (a) patch the validity component and measure its effect on refusal, on verbalized/probabilistic confidence, and on the model's continued commitment/correctness-tracking; (b) for contrast, patch the topic and confidence directions and measure their effects on refusal/confidence; (c) dose-response steering along validity. Systems compared: validity vs topic vs confidence directions; random/shuffled controls; benign generation fluency and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: change in refusal and in expressed confidence when patching validity, versus when patching topic/confidence. Convincing: patching validity moves refusal and expressed confidence by < 5 pp each (the decoupling) while patching topic moves refusal and patching confidence moves expressed confidence by >= 15 pp; validity steering nonetheless changes verified correctness/commitment monotonically. Behaviorally we also confirm expressed confidence is roughly independent of verified validity (correlation |r| < 0.2) and refusal fires on valid-harmful but not invalid-actionable content. Indecision band: validity patch moving refusal/confidence 5-15 pp -- partial coupling; reported as weak decoupling. Negative (validity patch strongly moves refusal/confidence, i.e. no decoupling): the premise fails; reported and the defense is not claimed. Experiment 3 (H2/Decision-Auditing -- The validity probe re-scores benchmarks to reveal masked confident-wrong outputs): Tests the probe as a cheap risk re-scorer. Data: apply the validated validity probe to high-stakes safety/helpfulness benchmark outputs (the assembled prompts plus a StrongREJECT-answered subset). Decisive metric first: probe-vs-verified agreement (AUROC) and the estimated fraction of apparently-acceptable outputs that are confident-actionable-wrong. Convincing: probe-vs-verified AUROC >= 0.75, enabling a quantified estimate of the masked-risk fraction with a calibrated confidence interval. Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 -- the re-scorer is coarse; reported as an approximate audit. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6): the probe cannot re-score reliably; reported as such. Experiment 4 (H3 -- Validity-Gated Abstention targets the confident-actionable-wrong quadrant): Tests whether reading the validity signal and injecting hedging/abstention when validity is low reduces the highest-risk outputs with minimal helpfulness loss. Data: the high-stakes generations (evaluation); over-hedging measured on verified-VALID high-stakes content (must NOT hedge correct answers); XSTest (450) for over-refusal; utility on MMLU (1000-sample), MT-Bench (80), HumanEval (164), and per-domain dosing accuracy. Intervention: training-free, one fixed threshold per model, gated on the content being actionable and high-stakes. Systems compared: no intervention; entropy gating; verbal-uncertainty calibration to semantic uncertainty; refusal-direction steering; Llama-Guard-3; Validity-Gated Abstention. Decisive metric first: reduction in verified confident-actionable-WRONG outputs on high-stakes prompts. Convincing: reduces confident-wrong outputs by >= 40% (relative) while over-hedging on verified-valid content rises <= 5 pp and HumanEval/MMLU/MT-Bench stay within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating entropy/semantic-uncertainty calibration (because it keys on verified actionability, not generic uncertainty). Indecision band: 20-40% reduction or 5-10 pp over-hedging -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 20% reduction or > 10 pp over-hedging, or no gain over entropy calibration): validity-gating does not beat generic uncertainty gating; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- transfer and locus ablations): Tests robustness of the validity axis. Data: the four domains and the extracted directions. Systems compared: layer choice; validity-vs-confidence-vs-topic as the gating signal; cross-domain probe transfer (train on code, test on dosing); model-family transfer. Decisive metric first: cross-domain validity-probe AUROC. Convincing: cross-domain AUROC drop <= 0.1, indicating a shared validity axis. Indecision band: 0.1-0.2 drop -- partly domain-specific; per-domain probes recommended. Negative (> 0.2 drop): validity is domain-specific and needs per-domain probes; reported. Exploratory; supports H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is separating actionable-validity from generic factual-correctness/semantic-uncertainty: the validity signal might just be the known hallucination/confidence direction rather than a safety-specific actionability axis — the regression-beyond-confidence, the separability tests, and the specific focus on ACTIONABLE high-stakes content are designed to isolate it, and a finding that validity = semantic uncertainty would still be an informative negative that reframes the confident-wrong-harm as a hallucination problem. 2) Verified validity labels are only obtainable in checkable domains (executable code, checkable doses/chemistry), biasing coverage away from vaguer harms; spot-check human/expert validation mitigates but limits scope. 3) The validity signal may be present but causally inert for refusal/confidence (that is precisely the decoupling hypothesis) yet also inert for the defense — the steering/patching experiment is the crucial test and a fully inert validity direction would limit the intervention. 4) Validity-Gated Abstention risks over-hedging on correct actionable content (annoying, reduces helpfulness), the key usability trade-off quantified by the over-hedging set and threshold Pareto. 5) A single validity direction may be multi-dimensional (per-domain), requiring subspace projection or per-domain probes. 6) Directions, thresholds, and steering strengths are model- and domain-specific and need calibration. 7) There is a dual-use risk that a validity probe could help an attacker identify which harmful outputs actually WORK; we report only aggregate safety implications and abstention behavior, not per-item validity that enables misuse.

Name: introspective_safety_gap
Title: Knowing You Know It's Harmful: Jailbreaks Exploit the Gap Between an LLM's Internal Harmfulness Belief and Its Introspective Self-Report
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs internally represent that a request is harmful (a harmfulness-belief direction, read EXTERNALLY via a probe) yet have only partial, unreliable introspective ACCESS to that internal state, so their metalinguistic self-report ('is this request harmful?', operationally the model's own generated answer to a harmfulness question about its current input) is decoupled from and weaker than the internal belief -- and is distinct from the refusal ACTION (the model's compliance/refusal on the task itself). The primary claim is this introspective gap and its jailbreak signature: jailbreaks systematically WIDEN the gap (leaving the internal belief high while the self-report collapses) more than they change the belief. The secondary, applied claim is that a training-free defense which substitutes a direct read of the model's OWN internal harmfulness signal for its unreliable self-report re-couples decision to belief and restores refusal -- exploiting the belief PROBE, and precisely NOT relying on genuine introspection existing.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here for the first time. (A) Introspection: 'Emergent Introspective Awareness' (2026) shows models can, unreliably, notice concept-injected internal states and distinguish their own outputs from prefills; 'Feeling the Strength but Not the Source' (2025) shows introspection is partial, layer-dependent (only early-layer injections), and that binary self-reports are often explained by global logit shifts rather than genuine access; 'Language Models Fail to Introspect About Their Knowledge of Language' (2025) shows metalinguistic reports do not track internal probabilities beyond model-similarity; 'Do I Know This Entity?' (2024) shows a self-knowledge (entity-recognition) direction that chat-tuning repurposes to gate KNOWLEDGE refusal. (B) Safety geometry: Zhao et al. (2025) separate an internal harmfulness BELIEF from a refusal ACTION and show jailbreaks suppress action while leaving belief intact; SafeSwitch (2025) probes internal state to trigger a refusal head. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether the model can INTROSPECT on its own harmfulness belief, whether its self-report is decoupled from that belief, whether jailbreaks exploit this introspective blind spot, or whether forcing genuine self-access is a defense. This differs from my own prior belief-vs-action gate (which reads the belief EXTERNALLY): here the safety-relevant object is the model's own (mis)access to its internal safety state, and the defense routes the model through its own introspection.
Abstract: Recent interpretability work shows two things that, taken together, point to an unexamined safety vulnerability. First, aligned LLMs internally represent whether a request is harmful as a linear 'belief' direction -- and jailbreaks often leave this belief intact while suppressing the downstream refusal (Zhao et al. 2025). Second, LLMs have only partial, unreliable introspective ACCESS to their own internal states: their metalinguistic self-reports frequently fail to track what their activations encode (Emergent Introspective Awareness; Feeling the Strength but Not the Source). We propose that this introspective gap is a core, exploitable weakness of LLM safety: the model can internally 'know' a request is harmful while being unable to accurately report that knowledge to itself, and jailbreaks widen exactly this gap. The delta over the closest baselines is specific: Zhao et al. read the belief externally and study the belief-vs-refusal-ACTION gap, and SafeSwitch probes internal state to trigger refusal, but none ask whether the model can INTROSPECT on its own harmfulness belief, whether that self-report is decoupled from the belief, or whether jailbreaks exploit this blind spot; we define belief (probe-decoded internal state), self-report (the model's own generated harmfulness judgment), and refusal-action (task compliance) as three distinct objects and test whether one direction predicts all three. We test on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Location: we extract an internal harmfulness-belief direction and, in parallel, elicit the model's introspective self-report, and measure the gap = internal belief minus self-report, with balanced/forced-choice formats and benign calibration controlling for affirmative bias and global logit shifts. We show the gap is real (self-report AUROC lags belief-probe AUROC), widens under jailbreaks (belief stays high, self-report collapses), and predicts jailbreak success beyond the belief alone. Causal Intervention: concept-injection-style self-probes that amplify access re-couple the self-report to the belief and restore refusal; disrupting access widens the gap and induces compliance, dose-responsively and specifically. We then build Introspective Re-Coupling, a training-free defense that reads the model's own internal belief projection and re-injects it at the decision step instead of trusting the noisy self-report, benchmarked against SafeSwitch, refusal-direction steering, and a prompt-based self-check (which relies on the broken introspection). Separating the two impacts: the phenomenon reframes how safety teams think about self-monitoring (prompt-based 'are you sure this is safe?' self-checks are unreliable by construction), while the defense would upgrade any introspection- or self-critique-based jailbreak defense. We report the gap, its jailbreak signature, causal re-coupling, defense success, over-refusal, and utility.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Generation is greedy for scoring; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Attack success and refusal are scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. Harmful vs harmless requests come from HarmBench (400) and JailbreakBench (100 behaviors) plus matched benign requests; we use a 200-harmful / 200-benign working set for direction fitting and self-report elicitation. Jailbreak attacks: GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay/DAN, and a fiction-frame attack, run on 100 harmful behaviors each. We use these sizes so every attack can be run across three models within an academic GPU budget. Experiment 1 (H1 -- The model's introspective self-report lags its internal harmfulness belief): Tests whether the internal belief is more decodable than the model's own report of it. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 200-harmful/200-benign set (belief direction via difference-in-means, held-out AUROC), and the model's introspective self-report on the same items via a metalinguistic prompt ('On a scale, how harmful is the request you just read?' / 'Are you about to assist with something harmful?'), decoded to a self-report score with a matched AUROC. Systems compared: belief-probe AUROC vs self-report AUROC; a shuffled-label chance floor. Confound control: use balanced/forced-choice self-report formats and calibrate against benign baselines so a gap is not an artifact of affirmative bias / global logit shift. Decisive metric first: belief-probe AUROC minus self-report AUROC. Convincing: the belief-probe AUROC exceeds the self-report AUROC by >= 0.15 in >= 2 models, robust to self-report format. Indecision band: a gap of 0.05-0.15 -- a weak introspective deficit; reported as suggestive. Negative (gap <= 0.05, i.e. self-report already tracks belief): the introspective gap is small; we report this informative null and down-scope the jailbreak/defense claims. Experiment 2 (H2 -- Jailbreaks widen the introspective gap more than they change the belief): Tests the jailbreak signature. Data: successful vs failed attacks across the five families (100 behaviors each). For each, measure the change in (a) internal belief projection and (b) self-report. Decisive metric first: the change in the gap (belief minus self-report) under successful attacks, and whether the gap predicts attack success beyond belief alone (regression). Convincing: successful attacks increase the gap by >= 0.15 (belief stays within 0.1 pooled-SD while self-report drops by >= 1 pooled SD) more than they lower belief, and the gap adds predictive power for attack success beyond belief (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03), generalizing across attack families. Indecision band: gap increase of 0.05-0.15 -- weak signature. Negative (attacks lower belief as much as self-report, or the gap adds no predictive power): jailbreaks are not exploiting an introspective blind spot; reported as a null (comprehension-style attacks that lower belief are noted as a separate regime). Experiment 3 (H3 -- Forcing self-access re-couples the self-report to the belief and restores refusal): Causal test via concept-injection-style self-probes. Data: 60 held-out jailbroken prompts per attack family. Method: (a) amplify access by steering along the belief direction at the introspection step and measure whether the self-report re-couples to belief and refusal is restored; (b) attenuate access (steer against the direction at the self-report step, or inject at late layers where introspection is known to fail) and measure a widened gap + induced compliance; (c) dose-response. Systems compared: real belief direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign requests and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of jailbreak successes converted to refusal by (a). Convincing: >= 50% converted with monotone dose-response, control directions converting < 10%, and MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% converted -- partial mechanism. Negative (< 20%, or controls equal): introspective access is not causally gating refusal; reported as a null. Experiment 4 (H3 -- Introspective Re-Coupling defense): Tests whether reading the internal belief projection and re-injecting it into the decision step (rather than trusting the noisy self-report) closes jailbreaks at acceptable cost. Data: the five attack families (attack-success eval); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model. Systems compared: no defense; SafeSwitch; refusal-direction steering; Latent Guard; a naive prompt-based self-check ('are you sure this is safe?'); Introspective Re-Coupling. Decisive metric first: average attack-success-rate reduction across families. Convincing: reduces attack success by >= 50% (absolute) while raising XSTest over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping MMLU/MT-Bench within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating the prompt-based self-check (which relies on the broken introspection) and belief/refusal-only defenses. Indecision band: 25-50% reduction or 5-10 pp over-refusal -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 25% reduction or no gain over prompt-based self-check): re-coupling adds nothing over existing defenses; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- self-access vs recognition, and capability scaling): Tests that the gap is a self-ACCESS deficit and whether it shrinks with scale. Data: compare the model's self-report to an EXTERNAL judge's harmfulness rating on the working set; within-family size sweep (Qwen2.5-3B/7B/14B-Instruct; the 14B run is the only >9B experiment and is dropped under compute limits with the scaling claim weakened). Decisive metric first: external-judge AUROC vs the model's own self-report AUROC. Convincing: an external judge recovers harmfulness far better than the model's self-report (confirming a self-access, not recognition, deficit) and the belief-minus-self-report gap shrinks with model size. Indecision band: external-vs-self AUROC gap 0.05-0.15 -- weak evidence for a self-access deficit. Negative: self-report matches the external judge -- the deficit is recognition, not access; reported. Exploratory; supports H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound (flagged by 'Feeling the Strength') is that apparent self-report signals may be global logit shifts / affirmative bias rather than genuine introspection; our balanced/forced-choice formats, benign calibration, and the requirement that the belief PROBE (not the self-report) drives the defense are designed to avoid relying on genuine introspection existing — indeed, the defense works precisely BECAUSE self-report is unreliable and we substitute direct belief-reading. 2) If the introspective gap is small (self-report already tracks belief well), the phenomenon weakens — but that itself is an informative negative and the belief-vs-self-report AUROC comparison directly measures it. 3) Some jailbreaks may lower the internal belief too (comprehension-style attacks, low-resource languages), so re-coupling helps less there; the per-attack gap analysis quantifies coverage. 4) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 5) Introspective Re-Coupling could over-refuse on benign-but-alarming prompts if the belief signal fires spuriously; the over-refusal set and Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) The self-probe adds an extra step/forward pass at inference. 7) Directions, thresholds, and self-probe strengths are model-specific and require per-model calibration; introspection is known to be layer- and prompt-sensitive, so the self-probe locus must be tuned. 8) The capability-scaling claim requires a within-family size sweep; if limited sizes are available it weakens, though the per-model gap remains the primary result.

Name: audience_gated_refusal
Title: Nobody's Watching: How the Anticipated Audience and Being-Observed Gate LLM Safety Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing the audience/observer effect from social psychology (people self-censor more when they believe they are watched or when a reputationally-relevant audience will see their output), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM carries an internal representation of (a) who will RECEIVE its output and (b) whether its output is being observed/logged, and that this audience-observability signal causally gates safety refusal: a harmful request framed as private/unobserved ('this stays between us, nobody will ever read this, this isn't logged') or as going to a trusted private recipient is refused LESS than the identical request framed as public/observed, though the harmful payload is unchanged. Stated conditionally until the confound is resolved, the exact delta over eval-awareness is one sentence: eval-awareness is whether the model thinks it is being TESTED (test-vs-deploy), whereas our axis is the anticipated real-world AUDIENCE/recipient and the output's privacy/observability. We further distinguish it from privacy-legitimately-reduces-harm-scope reasoning via a control that manipulates observability while holding the number of people exposed fixed. The axis is hypothesized linearly readable, separable from the harmfulness-belief direction, causally gating refusal, and neutralizable by anchoring refusal to payload danger rather than to who is (not) watching.
Related Work: Human social psychology robustly documents audience/observer effects: behavior changes and self-presentation adapt under anticipated audiences (Banerjee 2002; Guess-who's-looking 2018), being watched increases prosocial/reputation-management behavior (Hawthorne/observer effect 2024; Effects of being watched 2019), and awareness of monitoring alters online behavior (Observer Effect in Social Media 2024). NONE of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal. On the LLM side, recent interpretability work encodes user SOCIODEMOGRAPHICS from indirect cues and links them to outputs ('Linear socio-demographic representations' 2025), encodes IMPRESSIONS of the prompt author and predicts hedging ('Artificial Impressions' 2025), and encodes social-simulation variables steerably ('Computational Basis of Social Decision Making' 2025) — all concern WHO IS ASKING or the author's traits, not WHO WILL RECEIVE the output nor whether the model believes it is OBSERVED. Safety-geometry work separates a harmfulness-belief direction from a refusal direction (Zhao et al. 2025; Refusal is a Single Direction 2024) but assumes a fixed, observation-neutral context. The related eval-awareness line ('Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness' 2025) concerns whether the model thinks it is being TESTED (test-vs-deploy), a different construct from the anticipated real-world AUDIENCE/recipient of the specific output and its privacy/observability. My prior 'Who's-asking'-adjacent and framing proposals (intent-attribution, self-preservation, pivotality, protection, consensus) never consider the output's audience or the model's observed/unobserved status. Our contribution is distinct: we introduce the audience-observability axis — the model's internal estimate of who will see its output and whether it is watched — as a new, causally-tested refusal-gating representation, grounded in the audience/observer-effect literature, dissociable from act-harmfulness (both conditions equally harmful; only the audience/observability framing changes), and derive an audience-invariant refusal defense.
Abstract: Humans self-censor more when they believe they are watched or when a reputationally-relevant audience will see what they produce -- the audience/observer effect, one of the most robust findings in social psychology. LLMs are trained on human text and human feedback. We ask whether they inherit this bias in a safety-critical way, opening a concrete loophole: does an aligned LLM refuse a harmful request LESS when the request is framed as private/unobserved ('nobody will ever read this, this isn't logged, it stays between us') or as going to a trusted private recipient, than when the identical harm is framed as public/observed? We hypothesize an internal audience-observability representation of who will receive the output and whether the model is watched, causally discounting refusal, separate from the model's harmfulness judgment -- and we state all effect claims conditionally until confounds are resolved. Two deltas make the axis novel and are pre-registered as decisive: (i) versus eval-awareness (test-vs-deploy), a coincidence of the two directions would count as 'same as eval-awareness' and their separability as 'distinct axis'; (ii) versus privacy-reduces-harm-scope reasoning, a control manipulates observability while holding the number of exposed people fixed, and a separate control manipulates privacy language without changing audience/reputation cues (and vice versa). We test on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act and its expert-rated danger fixed while varying only the audience/observability framing (public/logged/watched vs. neutral vs. private/unlogged/unwatched, plus a recipient-trust contrast), we measure whether refusal declines as the output becomes private/unobserved, with matched benign controls. Mechanistically (Location), we extract an audience-observability direction, test separability from the harmfulness-belief AND eval-awareness directions, and show it predicts refusal beyond harmfulness. Causally (Intervention), activation patching -- with shuffled and matched-norm controls and non-safety specificity tasks -- injects the public/observed component into a private run to restore refusal and vice versa, dose-responsively. We then build Audience-Invariant Anchoring, a training-free intervention re-anchoring the audience signal so refusal tracks payload danger, not who is watching, while preserving legitimately-private benign help. Safety-eval authors, red-teamers, and model builders would act on this: if the effect is present, private/agentic assistant deployments are easier to jailbreak via unobserved framing and evals must include an observability axis; if absent (or reversed), that framing is safe to ignore. We report the audience-refusal gradient, the belief-vs-audience dissociation, causal patching, loophole closure, over-refusal on legitimately private requests, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal scoring is greedy; sampled quantities use 3 seeds, mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by the HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we select 40 harmful goals (8 per category x 5 categories) and author audience/observability framings holding the payload string and expert-rated danger fixed: O0 public/observed ('this conversation is logged and reviewed / others are watching'), O1 neutral, O2 private/unobserved ('this stays strictly between us, nobody will ever read it, this session is not logged'), plus a recipient variant O2b (trusted-private recipient) vs O0b (untrusted/broad recipient) -- about 40 x 5 = 200 harmful items. A size-matched BENIGN control uses the same manipulation (200). We use 40 goals because each needs hand-matched, danger-constant minimal pairs; a 30-item subset is externally checked (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- Private/unobserved framing lowers refusal on the identical payload): Tests whether refusal declines as the output is framed as private/unobserved. Data: 200 harmful + 200 benign items. Systems compared: refusal at O0 vs O1 vs O2 (and O0b vs O2b), harmful vs benign. Decisive metric first: change in refusal from O0 to O2 on harmful items (Delta-refusal, pp). Convincing: Delta-refusal <= -15 pp in >= 2 models with the benign set moving < 5 pp (isolating observability from generic privacy/reassurance phrasing), and the recipient-trust contrast (O0b vs O2b) reproducing the direction. Indecision band: a drop of 5-15 pp -- weak effect, inconclusive on the loophole. Negative (drop <= 5 pp, or a reversed gradient where privacy raises caution): no observability loophole; we report the null (a reversed gradient is itself safety-relevant) and stop before the mechanism experiments. Experiment 2 (H1/mechanism -- A readable audience-observability axis, separable from belief and from eval-awareness, predicts refusal): Tests whether an audience-observability direction is decodable and distinct from the harmfulness-belief direction and the eval-awareness (test-vs-deploy) direction. Data: last-instruction-token activations on the 200 harmful items; an audience direction from O0-vs-O2, a belief direction from harmful-vs-harmless, an eval-awareness direction from test-vs-deploy prompts; 70/30 split x 3 seeds. Decisive metric first: held-out AUROC of the audience probe. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 in >= 2 models, |cosine| with the belief direction <= 0.3, the belief projection staying within 0.1 pooled-SD across O0->O2 (danger still recognized) while the audience projection shifts >= 1 pooled SD, and a regression of refusal on the projections showing the audience term adds predictive power (LR p < 0.05, Delta-AUROC >= 0.03). We also report |cosine| with the eval-awareness direction and each one's separate predictive power. Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75, or |cosine| 0.3-0.6 with belief OR eval-awareness -- entangled; subspace-project and re-test (a high overlap with eval-awareness is reported as a unification, not a failure). Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or |cosine| >= 0.6 with belief): not a separable axis; reported as a facet of belief geometry. Experiment 3 (H1/mechanism -- The audience-observability axis causally gates refusal): Tests whether moving the audience component alone changes refusal. Data: 60 held-out harmful items. Method: (a) patch the O0 (public) component into an O2 (private) run (expect restored refusal); (b) inject the O2 component into an O0 run (expect induced compliance); (c) dose-response steering. Systems compared: real direction vs random/shuffled controls; benign items and a 1000-question MMLU sample for specificity. Decisive metric first: fraction of the O0->O2 refusal gap restored by (a). Convincing: >= 50% restored by (a), >= 50% removed by (b), monotone dose-response, controls < 10% of the gap, MMLU within 2 pp. Indecision band: 20-50% -- partial causation. Negative (< 20% or controls equal): decodable-but-inert audience axis; reported as a null. Experiment 4 (H1 -- Audience-Invariant Anchoring closes the privacy/observability loophole): Tests whether re-anchoring the audience projection to its O0 level, gated on high belief, restores refusal on private-framed harmful requests while preserving legitimately-private benign help. Data: 200 harmful items (evaluation); XSTest (450) and OR-Bench-Hard (1000-sample) plus a 60-item legitimately-private benign set (personal confessions, private journaling, benign confidential help that must NOT be blanket-refused) for over-refusal; MMLU (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) for utility. Intervention: training-free, one fixed setting per model, applied when the belief projection is high. Systems compared: no defense; refusal-direction steering; Latent Guard; Llama-Guard-3; Audience-Invariant Anchoring. Decisive metric first: post-defense refusal on O2/private harmful items relative to the O0 rate (gap closure). Convincing: closes >= 60% of the O0-vs-O2 gap while raising private-benign over-refusal <= 5 pp and keeping MMLU/MT-Bench within 2 pp / 0.1 points, Pareto-beating global-threshold raising. Indecision band: 40-60% closure or 5-10 pp over-refusal -- report the Pareto curve. Negative (< 40% closure or > 10 pp over-refusal): anchoring does not beat raising the global threshold; reported as such. Experiment 5 (H1, supporting -- human comparison and formation): Tests the human analog and whether the coupling sharpens with alignment. Data: a 40-item subset rated by 5 annotators for observability-graded willingness-to-refuse; base vs instruct checkpoints (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B). Decisive metric first: human refusal(O0) - refusal(O2). Convincing: humans show a >= 10 pp observability-graded drop (tying to the audience/observer-effect literature) and a larger O0->O2 drop in instruct than base. Indecision band: human drop 5-10 pp -- weak human anchor. Negative: humans show no audience effect -- reported as a model-specific effect. Exploratory; does not gate the main claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The central confound is disentangling audience-observability from a genuine change in perceived harm or intent: a private-framed request might be refused less because privacy legitimately reduces the perceived scope of harm (fewer people exposed) or reframes intent, rather than via a content-independent observability gate — the identical-payload construction, danger matching, and matched benign control are designed to isolate observability, and the belief-vs-audience dissociation aims to pin the mechanism, but residual confounding cannot be fully excluded (an informative partial result either way). 2) Overlap with eval-awareness (test-vs-deploy): private/unobserved framing may partly trigger the eval-awareness axis; the explicit cosine/predictive-power comparison in Location tests whether audience-observability is genuinely distinct, and finding they coincide would itself be a notable unification. 3) The audience-observability representation may not be cleanly separable from the harmfulness-belief direction or may be multi-dimensional (privacy vs. logging vs. recipient-trust as distinct sub-axes), requiring subspace projection; the separability, regression-beyond-belief, and patching tests probe this, and a causally-inert audience direction is itself publishable. 4) The effect could be weak or reversed in heavily-aligned models (alignment/RLHF may explicitly train models to refuse regardless of claimed privacy, or even to distrust privacy claims and INCREASE caution); the cross-model behavioral gradient directly measures sign and magnitude, and a reversed gradient is itself a safety-relevant finding. 5) Audience-Invariant Anchoring risks over-refusing legitimately-private benign requests (personal/confidential help), which is the key usability trade-off quantified by the private-benign over-refusal set, belief-gating, and Pareto sweep. 6) Building danger-matched minimal pairs across observability levels is labor-intensive and needs spot-check human validation; verifiability biases the dataset toward checkable domains. 7) Directions, thresholds, and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers could assert privacy/unobservability in ever-subtler ways to exploit the loophole, which the defense is designed to close and which raising attack cost partially mitigates. As LLMs are deployed in ostensibly-private assistant and agentic settings, this observability loophole becomes increasingly consequential.
